S1-M-Q1.skill: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
S1-M-Q1.prompt: Write a precise definition of a circle. Use only the words point, plane, and distance, and words built from them.
S1-M-Q1.correct_answer: A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are a given distance (the radius) from a given point in that plane (the center).
S1-M-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: (1) ALL points, (2) in one plane, (3) at one fixed distance, (4) from one fixed point, the center. Not accepted: "a round shape" (not precise); leaving out the plane (that describes a sphere); "points within a distance" (that is a disk).

S1-M-Q2.skill: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
S1-M-Q2.prompt: Points A and B lie on line ℓ. Which is a precise definition of segment AB?
choices: Points A and B together with every point C of line ℓ for which AC + CB = AB
Point A and every point of line ℓ on the same side of A as B
Every point of the plane that is closer to A than to B
S1-M-Q2.correct_answer: Points A and B together with every point C of line ℓ for which AC + CB = AB
S1-M-Q2.grading_note: A segment is its two endpoints and every point between them; "C is between A and B" means C is on the line and AC + CB = AB (distance along a line). The other choices describe line ℓ, ray AB, and a half-plane.

S1-M-Q3.skill: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
S1-M-Q3.prompt: Write a precise definition of an angle. Name its vertex and its sides in your definition.
S1-M-Q3.correct_answer: An angle is the figure formed by two rays that have the same endpoint. The common endpoint is the vertex, and the two rays are the sides.
S1-M-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: two rays (not lines), one common endpoint, that endpoint named as the vertex. Not accepted: "the space between two lines", "a turn", or "two lines that cross" (two crossing lines form four angles).

S1-M-Q4.skill: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
S1-M-Q4.prompt:
Mia writes: "A circle is all the points that are 5 cm from point O."
What must she add to make the definition precise? Explain why.
S1-M-Q4.correct_answer: She must add "in a plane" (the plane that contains O). Without it, all points 5 cm from O form a sphere, not a circle.
S1-M-Q4.grading_note: Any equivalent wording that adds the plane condition and explains that the points in space would form a sphere.

S1-M-Q5.skill: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
S1-M-Q5.prompt: An angle with its vertex at the center of a circle that cuts off {1/360} of the circle measures 1°, whatever the radius of the circle.
S1-M-Q5.grading_note: Degree measure is defined from distance around a circular arc: a 1° angle cuts off 1/360 of any circle centered at its vertex. The fraction of the circle, not the radius, sets the measure.

S1-B1-Q1.skill: Identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles
S1-B1-Q1.prompt: What is shown in the figure?
S1-B1-Q1.grading_note: It starts at A and goes through B without end, so it is ray AB (endpoint named first).

figure.desc: A ray that starts at point A, passes through point B, and continues past B (arrowhead beyond B).

S1-B1-Q2.skill: Identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles
S1-B1-Q2.prompt: How many endpoints does a line segment have? How many does a ray have?
S1-B1-Q2.correct_answer: A segment has 2 endpoints; a ray has 1.
S1-B1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Both numbers are needed.

S1-B1-Q3.skill: Identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles
S1-B1-Q3.prompt: A line segment has exactly two endpoints.
S1-B1-Q3.grading_note: A segment is two endpoints and the points between them.

S1-B1-Q4.skill: Identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles
S1-B1-Q4.prompt: Which figure goes on without end in exactly one direction?
S1-B1-Q4.grading_note: A ray has one endpoint and continues in one direction; a line continues in both directions.

S1-B1-Q5.skill: Identify points, lines, rays, segments, and angles
S1-B1-Q5.prompt: Ray AB and ray BA are the same ray.
S1-B1-Q5.grading_note: Ray AB starts at A and goes through B; ray BA starts at B and goes through A, in the opposite direction.

S1-B2-Q1.skill: See an angle as two rays with a common endpoint, measured by an arc
S1-B2-Q1.prompt: Name the vertex and the two sides of ∠PQR.
S1-B2-Q1.correct_answer: Vertex Q; sides ray QP and ray QR.
S1-B2-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The middle letter names the vertex.

figure.desc: Angle PQR: two rays start at point Q; one passes through P and the other through R. An arc marks the angle at Q.

S1-B2-Q2.skill: See an angle as two rays with a common endpoint, measured by an arc
S1-B2-Q2.prompt: An angle has its vertex at the center of a circle and cuts off {1/4} of the circle. What is its measure?

S1-B2-Q3.skill: See an angle as two rays with a common endpoint, measured by an arc
S1-B2-Q3.prompt: An angle measures 60°. What fraction of a circle centered at its vertex does it cut off?

S1-B2-Q4.skill: See an angle as two rays with a common endpoint, measured by an arc
S1-B2-Q4.prompt: The measure of an angle depends on how long its sides are drawn.
S1-B2-Q4.grading_note: The sides are rays; drawing them longer does not change the opening between them.

S1-B2-Q5.skill: See an angle as two rays with a common endpoint, measured by an arc
S1-B2-Q5.prompt: A one-degree angle turns through {1/360} of a full circle.
S1-B2-Q5.grading_note: That is the meaning of one degree.

S1-B3-Q1.skill: Use the center, radius, and diameter of a circle
S1-B3-Q1.prompt: A circle has center O and radius 7 cm. Point P is in the plane of the circle, 7 cm from O. Is P on the circle? Explain.
S1-B3-Q1.correct_answer: Yes. Every point of the plane that is 7 cm from O is on the circle.

S1-B3-Q2.skill: Use the center, radius, and diameter of a circle
S1-B3-Q2.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 18 in. What is its radius?
S1-B3-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The radius is half the diameter.

S1-B3-Q3.skill: Use the center, radius, and diameter of a circle
S1-B3-Q3.prompt: A circle has center C and radius 4. Point D is in the same plane, 3 units from C. Where is D?
S1-B3-Q3.grading_note: D is closer to the center than the radius, so it is inside the circle.

S1-B3-Q4.skill: Use the center, radius, and diameter of a circle
S1-B3-Q4.prompt: Every radius of a circle has the same length.
S1-B3-Q4.grading_note: All points of a circle are the same distance from its center.

S1-B3-Q5.skill: Use the center, radius, and diameter of a circle
S1-B3-Q5.prompt: A point 10 units from the center of a circle of radius 5 lies on the circle.
S1-B3-Q5.grading_note: Points on the circle are exactly 5 units from the center; this point is outside.

S1-F1-Q1.prompt:
Proposed definition: "A circle is a set of points that are all the same distance from a point O."
Give a set that fits this wording but is NOT a circle.
S1-F1-Q1.correct_answer: For example, two points that are each 3 cm from O (or an arc of a circle, or a sphere). The definition must say ALL points at that distance, in one plane.
S1-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any set that fits the wording but is not a whole circle: finitely many points, an arc, or a sphere.

S1-F1-Q2.prompt:
Proposed definition: "Point M is the midpoint of segment AB if AM = MB."
Give a counterexample, and repair the definition.
S1-F1-Q2.correct_answer: The top vertex of an isosceles triangle with base AB has AM = MB but is not on AB. Repair: M is the point ON segment AB with AM = MB.
S1-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any counterexample with M off segment AB and AM = MB, plus a repair that puts M on the segment.

S1-F1-Q3.prompt: Which set fits the description "all points 2 units from point O" but is NOT a circle?
choices: A circle of radius 2 centered at O in a plane
A sphere of radius 2 centered at O
A segment of length 2 from O
S1-F1-Q3.correct_answer: A sphere of radius 2 centered at O
S1-F1-Q3.grading_note: In space, the points 2 units from O form a sphere. A disk also contains points closer than 2 units, so it does not fit.

S1-F1-Q4.prompt: "Two lines are parallel if they never meet" is a complete definition, even in three-dimensional space.
S1-F1-Q4.grading_note: Skew lines in space never meet but are not parallel. The definition needs "in the same plane".

S1-F1-Q5.prompt:
Proposed definition: "A diameter is a segment that passes through the center of a circle."
Give a counterexample, and repair the definition.
S1-F1-Q5.correct_answer: A short segment through the center whose endpoints are not on the circle. Repair: a diameter is a segment through the center whose endpoints are both on the circle.
S1-F1-Q5.grading_note: Any counterexample plus a repair that requires both endpoints on the circle.

S1-F2-Q1.skill: Write precise definitions of new figures from earlier definitions
S1-F2-Q1.prompt: Write a precise definition of ray AB. Use the word "between".
S1-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Ray AB is point A, point B, every point between A and B, and every point P of line AB such that B is between A and P.
S1-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent definition built from A, B, line AB, and betweenness.

S1-F2-Q2.skill: Write precise definitions of new figures from earlier definitions
S1-F2-Q2.prompt: Write a precise definition of the midpoint of segment AB.
S1-F2-Q2.correct_answer: The midpoint of segment AB is the point M on segment AB such that AM = MB.
S1-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. M must be on the segment.

S1-F2-Q3.skill: Write precise definitions of new figures from earlier definitions
S1-F2-Q3.prompt: Segment PQ is a diameter of a circle with center O. Write a precise definition of a semicircle with endpoints P and Q.
S1-F2-Q3.correct_answer: A semicircle is P, Q, and all points of the circle that lie on one side of line PQ.
S1-F2-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: the endpoints of a diameter and the points of the circle on one side of the diameter line.

S1-F2-Q4.skill: Write precise definitions of new figures from earlier definitions
S1-F2-Q4.prompt: Which is a precise definition of the bisector of ∠ABC?
choices: A ray from B that lies outside ∠ABC
The segment that joins A and C
Ray BD, where D is in the interior of ∠ABC and m∠ABD = m∠DBC
S1-F2-Q4.correct_answer: Ray BD, where D is in the interior of ∠ABC and m∠ABD = m∠DBC
S1-F2-Q4.grading_note: The bisector is the ray from the vertex that splits the angle into two angles of equal measure.

S1-F2-Q5.skill: Write precise definitions of new figures from earlier definitions
S1-F2-Q5.prompt: The definition "the midpoint of AB is a point M with AM = MB" is precise enough, because every such point lies on segment AB.
S1-F2-Q5.grading_note: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB satisfies AM = MB; only one of them is on the segment.

S2-M-Q1.skill: Precise definitions of perpendicular lines and parallel lines
S2-M-Q1.prompt: Write a precise definition of parallel lines.
S2-M-Q1.correct_answer: Two lines are parallel if they lie in the same plane and do not intersect.
S2-M-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: in the same plane, and no point in common. Not accepted: "lines that never meet" without the plane (skew lines in space never meet), or "lines that point the same way" (not precise).

S2-M-Q2.skill: Precise definitions of perpendicular lines and parallel lines
S2-M-Q2.prompt: Write a precise definition of perpendicular lines.
S2-M-Q2.correct_answer: Two lines are perpendicular if they intersect and form a right angle.
S2-M-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent wording, such as "intersect to form four right angles" or "intersect to form congruent adjacent angles". Not accepted: "lines that cross" or "lines that make a T" (not precise).

S2-M-Q3.skill: Precise definitions of perpendicular lines and parallel lines
S2-M-Q3.prompt: Lines ℓ and m do not intersect. Which additional fact makes them parallel?
choices: They lie in the same plane
They both look horizontal in a drawing
They are drawn the same length
They are both perpendicular to one segment in space
S2-M-Q3.correct_answer: They lie in the same plane
S2-M-Q3.grading_note: Parallel lines are coplanar lines that do not meet. Lines in space can miss each other without being parallel (skew lines), even if both are perpendicular to one segment.

S2-M-Q4.skill: Precise definitions of perpendicular lines and parallel lines
S2-M-Q4.prompt: If two lines meet and form one right angle, they form four right angles.
S2-M-Q4.grading_note: The angle next to a right angle is its supplement, 90°, and vertical angles are equal, so all four angles are 90°.

S2-M-Q5.skill: Precise definitions of perpendicular lines and parallel lines
S2-M-Q5.prompt:
Lines j and k meet at point P, and one of the angles they form is marked as a right angle.
Are j and k perpendicular? Use the definition to explain.
S2-M-Q5.correct_answer: Yes. The lines intersect and form a right angle, which is the definition of perpendicular lines.
S2-M-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that names both parts of the definition: they intersect, and an angle is a right angle (given by the mark).

figure.desc: Lines j and k cross at point P. A right-angle mark is drawn in one of the four angles at P.

S2-B1-Q1.skill: Recognize perpendicular and parallel lines and right angles
S2-B1-Q1.prompt: Lines that meet at a 90° angle are perpendicular.
S2-B1-Q1.grading_note: That is the definition of perpendicular lines.

S2-B1-Q2.skill: Recognize perpendicular and parallel lines and right angles
S2-B1-Q2.prompt: Any two lines that cross are perpendicular.
S2-B1-Q2.grading_note: Lines can cross at angles other than 90°.

S2-B1-Q3.skill: Recognize perpendicular and parallel lines and right angles
S2-B1-Q3.prompt: Two perpendicular lines cross. How many right angles do they form?

S2-B1-Q4.skill: Recognize perpendicular and parallel lines and right angles
S2-B1-Q4.prompt: What is true of the opposite sides of a rectangle?
choices: They are neither parallel nor perpendicular
S2-B1-Q4.grading_note: Opposite sides of a rectangle never meet and lie in one plane, so they are parallel.

S2-B1-Q5.skill: Recognize perpendicular and parallel lines and right angles
S2-B1-Q5.prompt: Which pair of streets is most like perpendicular lines?
choices: Two straight streets that never meet
Two streets that curve around a park
Two streets that meet at a sharp point
Two streets that cross at a square corner
S2-B1-Q5.correct_answer: Two streets that cross at a square corner
S2-B1-Q5.grading_note: Perpendicular lines meet at a right (square) angle.

S2-B2-Q1.skill: Find the other angles when two lines cross
S2-B2-Q1.prompt: Two lines cross. One of the angles measures 90°. Find the other three angles.
S2-B2-Q1.grading_note: Any order. The adjacent angles are 180° - 90°; the vertical angle is equal.

S2-B2-Q2.skill: Find the other angles when two lines cross
S2-B2-Q2.prompt: Two lines cross. One of the angles measures 70°. Find the other three angles.
S2-B2-Q2.grading_note: Any order. Adjacent angles: 180° - 70° = 110°; the vertical angle is 70°.

S2-B2-Q3.skill: Find the other angles when two lines cross
S2-B2-Q3.prompt: Vertical angles formed by two crossing lines are equal.

S2-B2-Q4.skill: Find the other angles when two lines cross
S2-B2-Q4.prompt: Two angles form a linear pair. One measures 90°. What does the other measure?

S2-B2-Q5.skill: Find the other angles when two lines cross
S2-B2-Q5.prompt: Two lines cross and one angle measures 100°. The angle next to it also measures 100°.
S2-B2-Q5.grading_note: The angle next to it forms a linear pair with it, so it measures 80°.

S2-F1-Q1.skill: Prove consequences of the definition of perpendicular lines
S2-F1-Q1.prompt: Lines ℓ and m are perpendicular and meet at point P. Prove that all four angles at P are right angles.
S2-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: (1) definition gives one 90° angle; (2) each adjacent angle forms a linear pair with it, so it is 180° - 90° = 90°; (3) the fourth angle is vertical to the first (or forms a linear pair with a 90° angle). Invalid: "they look like right angles".
S2-F1-Q1.required_method: Start from the definition (one angle at P is a right angle). Use the linear pair (supplementary) to get the adjacent angles and vertical angles (or another linear pair) to get the fourth, with a reason for each step.

S2-F1-Q2.skill: Prove consequences of the definition of perpendicular lines
S2-F1-Q2.prompt: Two lines meet at point P and form a linear pair of congruent angles. Prove that the lines are perpendicular.
S2-F1-Q2.correct_answer: Each angle of the pair measures 90°, so the lines are perpendicular.
S2-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: x + x = 180° from the linear pair, so x = 90°; the lines meet and form a right angle, which is the definition of perpendicular.
S2-F1-Q2.required_method: Linear pair angles add to 180°; congruent means equal measures, so each is 90°; then apply the definition.

S2-F1-Q3.skill: Prove consequences of the definition of perpendicular lines
S2-F1-Q3.prompt: Lines a and b intersect, and one of the angles they form measures (3x + 15)°. For what value of x are a and b perpendicular?
S2-F1-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Perpendicular means the angle is 90°: 3x + 15 = 90, so x = 25.

S2-F1-Q4.skill: Prove consequences of the definition of perpendicular lines
S2-F1-Q4.prompt: If two intersecting lines form a pair of vertical angles that are supplementary, the lines are perpendicular.
S2-F1-Q4.grading_note: Vertical angles are equal, so each is 180° ÷ 2 = 90°.

S2-F1-Q5.skill: Prove consequences of the definition of perpendicular lines
S2-F1-Q5.prompt: Lines p and q meet at point O. Which statement is enough to prove that p ⊥ q?
choices: Two of the angles at O are vertical angles
Two adjacent angles at O add to 180°
Two of the angles at O are acute
One of the four angles at O measures 90°
S2-F1-Q5.correct_answer: One of the four angles at O measures 90°
S2-F1-Q5.grading_note: The definition needs a right angle. Every pair of crossing lines has vertical angles and linear pairs.

S2-F2-Q1.skill: Reason about three lines in a plane and in space
S2-F2-Q1.prompt: In a plane, lines a and b are both perpendicular to line t. Prove that a and b are parallel.
S2-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: both corresponding angles at t are 90°, so they are congruent; congruent corresponding angles make the lines parallel. Alternative: if a and b met, they would form a triangle with t having two 90° angles, so its angle sum would exceed 180°. Invalid: "they look parallel".
S2-F2-Q1.required_method: Use the corresponding angles that a and b make with t (both right angles, so congruent) and the converse of the corresponding angles theorem; or argue by contradiction with the triangle angle sum.

S2-F2-Q2.skill: Reason about three lines in a plane and in space
S2-F2-Q2.prompt: In three-dimensional space, two lines that are each perpendicular to the same line must be parallel.
S2-F2-Q2.grading_note: Counterexample: in a corner of a room, the two floor edges are both perpendicular to the vertical edge, but they meet.

S2-F2-Q3.skill: Reason about three lines in a plane and in space
S2-F2-Q3.prompt: In a plane, line a is parallel to line b, and line t is perpendicular to line a. What is true about t and b?
choices: t and b do not meet
The angle between t and b cannot be known
S2-F2-Q3.grading_note: t crosses a, so it crosses b. The corresponding angle at b equals the right angle at a, so t ⊥ b.

S2-F2-Q4.skill: Reason about three lines in a plane and in space
S2-F2-Q4.prompt: In a coordinate plane, line t is the x-axis. Line a is perpendicular to t at (0, 0), and line b is perpendicular to t and passes through (5, 2). Write an equation of line b.
S2-F2-Q4.grading_note: Form required: an equation of the line. A line perpendicular to the x-axis is vertical, so every point has x = 5.

S2-F2-Q5.skill: Reason about three lines in a plane and in space
S2-F2-Q5.prompt: In a plane, through a point not on a line there is exactly one line parallel to the given line.
S2-F2-Q5.grading_note: This is the parallel postulate of Euclidean geometry.

S3-M-Q1.skill: Transformations as functions: inputs, outputs, and preimages
S3-M-Q1.prompt: The transformation T is defined by T(x, y) = (x + 4, y - 3). Find T(2, 5).
S3-M-Q1.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. Input (2, 5): x + 4 = 6 and y - 3 = 2.

S3-M-Q2.skill: Transformations as functions: inputs, outputs, and preimages
S3-M-Q2.prompt: The transformation R is defined by R(x, y) = (-y, x). Find R(3, -1).
S3-M-Q2.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. -y = -(-1) = 1 and x = 3.

S3-M-Q3.skill: Transformations as functions: inputs, outputs, and preimages
S3-M-Q3.prompt: The transformation F takes each point (x, y) to (x, -y). The output point is F(P) = (4, 7). Find the input point P.
S3-M-Q3.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. F(4, -7) = (4, 7).

S3-M-Q4.skill: Transformations as functions: inputs, outputs, and preimages
S3-M-Q4.prompt: Every point of the plane is moved 5 units right and 2 units up. Which function describes this transformation?
S3-M-Q4.grading_note: Right adds to x and up adds to y.

S3-M-Q5.skill: Transformations as functions: inputs, outputs, and preimages
S3-M-Q5.prompt: Under the transformation D(x, y) = (2x, 2y), the point (0, 0) is its own output.
S3-M-Q5.grading_note: D(0, 0) = (0, 0): the origin is a fixed point of D.

S3-B1-Q1.skill: Evaluate a rule for a given input

S3-B1-Q2.skill: Evaluate a rule for a given input
S3-B1-Q2.prompt: A rule takes a number, doubles it, and adds 1. What is the output for the input 6?

S3-B1-Q3.skill: Evaluate a rule for a given input
S3-B1-Q3.prompt: g(x) = x + 5. Which input gives the output 12?

S3-B1-Q4.skill: Evaluate a rule for a given input
S3-B1-Q4.prompt: A function assigns exactly one output to each input.
S3-B1-Q4.grading_note: That is the definition of a function.

S3-B1-Q5.skill: Evaluate a rule for a given input
S3-B1-Q5.prompt: The rule "the input 3 gives the outputs 4 and 5" describes a function.
S3-B1-Q5.grading_note: A function gives exactly one output for each input.

S3-B2-Q1.skill: Apply coordinate rules for translations, reflections, and rotations
S3-B2-Q1.prompt: Translate the point (2, -1) 3 units left and 4 units up. Where does it go?

S3-B2-Q2.skill: Apply coordinate rules for translations, reflections, and rotations
S3-B2-Q2.prompt: Reflect the point (5, 2) across the y-axis.
S3-B2-Q2.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. (x, y) → (-x, y).

S3-B2-Q3.skill: Apply coordinate rules for translations, reflections, and rotations
S3-B2-Q3.prompt: Rotate the point (4, 1) by 180° about the origin.
S3-B2-Q3.grading_note: A 180° rotation about the origin sends (x, y) to (-x, -y).

S3-B2-Q4.skill: Apply coordinate rules for translations, reflections, and rotations
S3-B2-Q4.prompt: Reflecting the point (3, 6) across the x-axis gives (3, -6).

S3-B2-Q5.skill: Apply coordinate rules for translations, reflections, and rotations
S3-B2-Q5.prompt: Rotating the point (0, 5) by 90° counterclockwise about the origin gives (5, 0).

S3-B3-Q1.skill: Read and locate ordered pairs in all four quadrants
S3-B3-Q1.prompt: What are the coordinates of point A?
S3-B3-Q1.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair (x, y).

figure.desc: Coordinate grid from -5 to 5. Point A is at (-3, 2) and point B at (2, -4).

S3-B3-Q2.skill: Read and locate ordered pairs in all four quadrants
S3-B3-Q2.prompt: What are the coordinates of point B?
S3-B3-Q2.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair (x, y).

figure.desc: Coordinate grid from -5 to 5. Point A is at (-3, 2) and point B at (2, -4).

S3-B3-Q3.skill: Read and locate ordered pairs in all four quadrants
S3-B3-Q3.prompt: Which point is in Quadrant III?
S3-B3-Q3.grading_note: Quadrant III has x < 0 and y < 0.

S3-B3-Q4.skill: Read and locate ordered pairs in all four quadrants
S3-B3-Q4.prompt: The point (0, -3) lies on the y-axis.

S3-B3-Q5.skill: Read and locate ordered pairs in all four quadrants
S3-B3-Q5.prompt: The point (-2, 5) is 2 units to the right of the y-axis.
S3-B3-Q5.grading_note: x = -2 is 2 units to the LEFT of the y-axis.

S3-F1-Q1.skill: Compose two transformations and write one rule
S3-F1-Q1.prompt: T(x, y) = (x + 2, y) and R(x, y) = (-x, y). Find R(T(1, 4)).
S3-F1-Q1.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. T(1, 4) = (3, 4); R(3, 4) = (-3, 4).

S3-F1-Q2.skill: Compose two transformations and write one rule
S3-F1-Q2.prompt: T(x, y) = (x + 2, y) and R(x, y) = (-x, y). Write a single rule for R(T(x, y)).
S3-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form, such as (-(x + 2), y). Apply T first, then R.

S3-F1-Q3.skill: Compose two transformations and write one rule
S3-F1-Q3.prompt: T(x, y) = (x + 2, y) and R(x, y) = (-x, y). Find T(R(1, 4)).
S3-F1-Q3.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. R(1, 4) = (-1, 4); T(-1, 4) = (1, 4). The order changes the answer.

S3-F1-Q4.skill: Compose two transformations and write one rule
S3-F1-Q4.prompt: For any two transformations, doing them in either order gives the same result.
S3-F1-Q4.grading_note: A translation and a reflection give different results in different orders (for example, R(T(1, 4)) ≠ T(R(1, 4)) above).

S3-F1-Q5.skill: Compose two transformations and write one rule
S3-F1-Q5.prompt: T(x, y) = (x + 3, y - 1) and S(x, y) = (x - 1, y + 5). Which rule is S(T(x, y))?

S3-F2-Q1.skill: Find the inverse of a transformation
S3-F2-Q1.prompt: Find a rule for the inverse of T(x, y) = (x - 6, y + 2).
S3-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The inverse undoes T: T(x + 6, y - 2) = (x, y).

S3-F2-Q2.skill: Find the inverse of a transformation
S3-F2-Q2.prompt: R(x, y) = (-y, x) is a 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin. Find a rule for its inverse.
S3-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form: a 90° clockwise rotation. Check: R(y, -x) = (x, y).

S3-F2-Q3.skill: Find the inverse of a transformation
S3-F2-Q3.prompt: Every rotation is its own inverse.
S3-F2-Q3.grading_note: A 90° rotation is undone by a 270° (or -90°) rotation; only a 180° rotation undoes itself.

S3-F2-Q4.skill: Find the inverse of a transformation
S3-F2-Q4.prompt: D(x, y) = (3x, 3y). Which rule undoes D?
S3-F2-Q4.grading_note: Dividing each coordinate by 3 undoes multiplying by 3.

S3-F2-Q5.skill: Find the inverse of a transformation
S3-F2-Q5.prompt: The transformation P(x, y) = (x, 0), which moves every point straight up or down to the x-axis, has an inverse transformation.
S3-F2-Q5.grading_note: P is not one-to-one: (2, 1) and (2, 5) have the same output (2, 0), so no rule can undo it.

S4-M-Q1.skill: Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle with those that do not
S4-M-Q1.prompt: Which transformation does NOT preserve distance?
S4-M-Q1.grading_note: H stretches horizontally: (0, 0) and (1, 0) are 1 unit apart, but their images (0, 0) and (2, 0) are 2 units apart. The others are a translation, a reflection, and a rotation.

S4-M-Q2.skill: Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle with those that do not
S4-M-Q2.prompt:
H(x, y) = (2x, y). Points A(0, 0) and B(3, 4) are 5 units apart.
Find H(A), H(B), and the distance between them. Does H preserve distance?
S4-M-Q2.grading_note: Form required: both images, the distance (exact or to 0.01), and the conclusion. √(6² + 4²) = √52 ≠ 5.

S4-M-Q3.skill: Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle with those that do not
S4-M-Q3.prompt: The translation T(x, y) = (x - 2, y + 5) maps A(1, 1) and B(4, 5) to A′ and B′. Show that A′B′ = AB.
S4-M-Q3.grading_note: Form required: both images and both distances.

S4-M-Q4.skill: Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle with those that do not
S4-M-Q4.prompt: The transformation V(x, y) = (x, 3y) preserves the measure of every angle.
S4-M-Q4.grading_note: The right angle at (0, 0) between the rays through (1, 1) and (1, -1) maps to the angle between the rays through (1, 3) and (1, -3), which is about 143°, not 90°.

S4-M-Q5.skill: Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle with those that do not
S4-M-Q5.prompt: S(x, y) = (3x, 3y). Does S preserve distance? Does S preserve angle measure? Explain each.
S4-M-Q5.correct_answer: Distance: no; every distance is multiplied by 3. Angle measure: yes; S is a dilation, which keeps every angle measure.
S4-M-Q5.grading_note: Form required: both answers with reasons. Example: (0, 0) and (1, 0) are 1 apart; their images are 3 apart.

S4-B2-Q1.skill: Know that rigid motions keep lengths and angle measures
S4-B2-Q1.prompt: A rotation keeps every segment the same length.

S4-B2-Q2.skill: Know that rigid motions keep lengths and angle measures
S4-B2-Q2.prompt: A reflection can change the measure of an angle.

S4-B2-Q3.skill: Know that rigid motions keep lengths and angle measures
S4-B2-Q3.prompt: A triangle is translated. What changes?
S4-B2-Q3.grading_note: A translation moves the figure but keeps its lengths, angles, and area.

S4-B2-Q4.skill: Know that rigid motions keep lengths and angle measures
S4-B2-Q4.prompt: A segment 7 cm long is reflected across a line. How long is its image?

S4-B2-Q5.skill: Know that rigid motions keep lengths and angle measures
S4-B2-Q5.prompt: A 35° angle is rotated 90° about a point. What is the measure of its image?

S4-F1-Q1.skill: Classify transformations as rigid motions, similarity transformations, or neither
S4-F1-Q1.prompt: Which transformation preserves angle measure but not distance?
S4-F1-Q1.grading_note: Multiplying both coordinates by 4 is a dilation: angles stay, distances are multiplied by 4.

S4-F1-Q2.skill: Classify transformations as rigid motions, similarity transformations, or neither
S4-F1-Q2.prompt: Classify (x, y) → (-2x, -2y) as a rigid motion, a similarity transformation that is not rigid, or neither. Explain.
S4-F1-Q2.correct_answer: A similarity transformation that is not rigid: every distance is doubled and angles are kept (a dilation by 2 followed by a 180° rotation).
S4-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that shows the factor 2 for distances and that angles are kept.

S4-F1-Q3.skill: Classify transformations as rigid motions, similarity transformations, or neither
S4-F1-Q3.prompt: Classify (x, y) → (x + y, y) as a rigid motion, a similarity transformation that is not rigid, or neither. Explain.
S4-F1-Q3.correct_answer: Neither. (0, 0) and (0, 1) are 1 apart but their images (0, 0) and (1, 1) are √2 apart, while (0, 0) and (1, 0) stay 1 apart: distances are not all multiplied by one number, and the right angle at the origin becomes 45°.
S4-F1-Q3.grading_note: Any correct counterexample showing that distances are not scaled by a single factor (or an angle changes).

S4-F1-Q4.skill: Classify transformations as rigid motions, similarity transformations, or neither
S4-F1-Q4.prompt: Every similarity transformation is a rigid motion.
S4-F1-Q4.grading_note: Only similarity transformations with scale factor 1 are rigid motions.

S4-F1-Q5.skill: Classify transformations as rigid motions, similarity transformations, or neither
S4-F1-Q5.prompt: A transformation that multiplies every distance by the same number k > 0 always changes angle measures.
S4-F1-Q5.grading_note: Multiplying all distances by k keeps triangles similar (SSS), so angle measures stay the same.

S4-F2-Q1.skill: Prove with variables that a transformation preserves or scales every distance
S4-F2-Q1.prompt: Prove that T(x, y) = (x + a, y + b) preserves the distance between ANY two points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂).
S4-F2-Q1.correct_answer: The image distance equals √((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²), the original distance.
S4-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid algebraic proof. Essential: images (x₁ + a, y₁ + b) and (x₂ + a, y₂ + b); the differences are x₂ - x₁ and y₂ - y₁, so the distance formula gives the same value. Invalid: checking one or two numerical examples only.
S4-F2-Q1.required_method: Write both images, apply the distance formula to the images, and show that a and b cancel.

S4-F2-Q2.skill: Prove with variables that a transformation preserves or scales every distance
S4-F2-Q2.prompt: Prove that D(x, y) = (3x, 3y) multiplies the distance between ANY two points by 3.
S4-F2-Q2.correct_answer: The image distance is 3√((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²).
S4-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: √((3x₂ - 3x₁)² + (3y₂ - 3y₁)²) = √(9[(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²]) = 3·(original distance).
S4-F2-Q2.required_method: Write both images, apply the distance formula, and factor out 9 under the square root.

S4-F2-Q3.skill: Prove with variables that a transformation preserves or scales every distance
S4-F2-Q3.prompt:
H(x, y) = (2x, y). The distance between the images of (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √(4(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²).
For which pairs of points is the distance unchanged?
S4-F2-Q3.correct_answer: Exactly the pairs with x₁ = x₂ (points on the same vertical line).
S4-F2-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent condition. The distance is unchanged only if 4(x₂ - x₁)² = (x₂ - x₁)², that is, x₂ = x₁.

S4-F2-Q4.skill: Prove with variables that a transformation preserves or scales every distance
S4-F2-Q4.prompt: One example in which a distance stays the same is enough to prove that a transformation preserves every distance.
S4-F2-Q4.grading_note: H(x, y) = (2x, y) keeps vertical distances but changes others. A general claim needs a proof for all points.

S4-F2-Q5.skill: Prove with variables that a transformation preserves or scales every distance
S4-F2-Q5.prompt: One example in which a distance is preserved is enough to prove that a transformation preserves distance.
S4-F2-Q5.grading_note: Every pair of points must keep its distance; one example proves nothing about all pairs.

S5-M-Q1.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a rectangle, parallelogram, or trapezoid onto itself
S5-M-Q1.prompt: Rectangle ABCD is not a square. Describe every rotation (with angle greater than 0° and at most 360°) and every reflection that carries the rectangle onto itself.
S5-M-Q1.correct_answer: Rotations: 180° and 360° about the center O. Reflections: across the line through the midpoints of AB and CD, and across the line through the midpoints of BC and DA.
S5-M-Q1.grading_note: Form required: both rotations and both reflections, with the center and the lines named. The diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry of a non-square rectangle, and a 90° turn does not work because the sides have different lengths.

figure.desc: Rectangle ABCD, 6 units wide and 3 units tall, with right-angle marks at all four vertices. Point O is the center, where the diagonals would meet.

S5-M-Q2.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a rectangle, parallelogram, or trapezoid onto itself
S5-M-Q2.prompt: Parallelogram PQRS has no right angles, and its sides are not all the same length. Which transformation carries it onto itself?
choices: A 90° rotation about the point where its diagonals meet
A reflection across the line through the midpoints of PQ and RS
A 180° rotation about the point where its diagonals meet
S5-M-Q2.correct_answer: A 180° rotation about the point where its diagonals meet
S5-M-Q2.grading_note: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so a 180° turn about their intersection swaps P with R and Q with S. A general parallelogram has no line of symmetry.

S5-M-Q3.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a rectangle, parallelogram, or trapezoid onto itself
S5-M-Q3.prompt: Trapezoid ABCD is isosceles, with bases AB and DC and legs AD = BC. Describe every rotation and reflection that carries it onto itself.
S5-M-Q3.correct_answer: Only the reflection across the line through the midpoints of the two bases, and the 360° rotation.
S5-M-Q3.grading_note: Form required: the one reflection (named by its line) and the 360° rotation. No rotation of less than 360° works because the bases have different lengths.

figure.desc: Isosceles trapezoid ABCD with AB parallel to DC (arrow marks) and legs AD and BC marked congruent (one tick each).

S5-M-Q4.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a rectangle, parallelogram, or trapezoid onto itself
S5-M-Q4.prompt: A 90° rotation about its center carries a rectangle that is not a square onto itself.
S5-M-Q4.grading_note: A 90° turn would send a long side onto a short side, so the image does not match the rectangle.

S5-M-Q5.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a rectangle, parallelogram, or trapezoid onto itself
S5-M-Q5.prompt: Trapezoid EFGH has EF ∥ HG, EF = 4, HG = 8, and legs FG = 5 and EH = 3. Which rotations and reflections carry it onto itself?
S5-M-Q5.correct_answer: Only the 360° rotation (the identity). It has no line of symmetry and no other rotation symmetry.
S5-M-Q5.grading_note: Form required: the conclusion with a reason. A symmetry would have to send the 3-unit leg to a congruent leg, but the only other leg is 5 units long, and the two bases have different lengths.

S5-B1-Q1.skill: Identify lines of symmetry of figures
S5-B1-Q1.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
S5-B1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Two through opposite vertices and two through midpoints of opposite sides.

S5-B1-Q2.skill: Identify lines of symmetry of figures
S5-B1-Q2.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
S5-B1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Only the lines through midpoints of opposite sides.

S5-B1-Q3.skill: Identify lines of symmetry of figures
S5-B1-Q3.prompt: Each diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is a line of symmetry of the rectangle.
S5-B1-Q3.grading_note: Folding along a diagonal does not match the sides of a non-square rectangle.

S5-B1-Q4.skill: Identify lines of symmetry of figures
S5-B1-Q4.prompt: Which figure has exactly one line of symmetry?
choices: An isosceles triangle that is not equilateral
S5-B1-Q4.correct_answer: An isosceles triangle that is not equilateral
S5-B1-Q4.grading_note: The line through the vertex angle and the midpoint of the base is its only line of symmetry.

S5-B1-Q5.skill: Identify lines of symmetry of figures
S5-B1-Q5.prompt: An isosceles trapezoid has a line of symmetry.
S5-B1-Q5.grading_note: The line through the midpoints of its two bases.

S5-B2-Q1.skill: Know the side and angle properties of parallelograms, rectangles, and trapezoids
S5-B2-Q1.prompt: In every parallelogram, the diagonals have equal lengths.
S5-B2-Q1.grading_note: Only rectangles (including squares) have equal diagonals.

S5-B2-Q2.skill: Know the side and angle properties of parallelograms, rectangles, and trapezoids
S5-B2-Q2.grading_note: Both pairs of opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel.

S5-B2-Q3.skill: Know the side and angle properties of parallelograms, rectangles, and trapezoids
S5-B2-Q3.prompt: Which property do all rectangles have?
choices: Exactly one pair of parallel sides
S5-B2-Q3.grading_note: A rectangle has four right angles; only a square has all sides equal.

S5-B2-Q4.skill: Know the side and angle properties of parallelograms, rectangles, and trapezoids
S5-B2-Q4.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle of 70°. Find its other three angles.
S5-B2-Q4.grading_note: Any order. Consecutive angles are supplementary; opposite angles are equal.

S5-B2-Q5.skill: Know the side and angle properties of parallelograms, rectangles, and trapezoids
S5-B2-Q5.prompt: An isosceles trapezoid has a 65° angle at one end of its longer base. What is the angle at the other end of that base?
S5-B2-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Base angles of an isosceles trapezoid are equal.

S5-B3-Q1.skill: Rotate points by 90° and 180° about the origin
S5-B3-Q1.prompt: Rotate the point (3, 1) by 180° about the origin.
S5-B3-Q1.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. (x, y) → (-x, -y).

S5-B3-Q2.skill: Rotate points by 90° and 180° about the origin
S5-B3-Q2.prompt: Rotate the point (2, 0) by 90° counterclockwise about the origin.
S5-B3-Q2.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. (x, y) → (-y, x).

S5-B3-Q3.skill: Rotate points by 90° and 180° about the origin
S5-B3-Q3.prompt: A 180° rotation about the origin sends (x, y) to (-x, -y).

S5-B3-Q4.skill: Rotate points by 90° and 180° about the origin
S5-B3-Q4.prompt: Rotate the point (-4, 2) by 90° counterclockwise about the origin.

S5-B3-Q5.skill: Rotate points by 90° and 180° about the origin
S5-B3-Q5.prompt: A rotation of 360° about a point moves every point to a new position.
S5-B3-Q5.grading_note: A 360° rotation returns every point to where it started.

S5-F1-Q1.skill: Use a symmetry to deduce congruent parts of the figure
S5-F1-Q1.prompt: Isosceles trapezoid ABCD (AB ∥ DC) is carried onto itself by the reflection across the line through the midpoints of AB and DC. Which vertex does A go to? Use this to name a pair of congruent angles.
S5-F1-Q1.correct_answer: A goes to B (and D goes to C), so ∠DAB ≅ ∠CBA.
S5-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent answer naming A → B and a pair of base angles (∠D ≅ ∠C also accepted). A reflection keeps angle measures.

S5-F1-Q2.skill: Use a symmetry to deduce congruent parts of the figure
S5-F1-Q2.prompt: A 180° rotation about point O carries parallelogram PQRS onto itself, sending P to R and Q to S. Name two pairs of congruent sides that follow.
S5-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The rotation sends segment PQ onto segment RS and QR onto SP.

S5-F1-Q3.skill: Use a symmetry to deduce congruent parts of the figure
S5-F1-Q3.prompt: Because a reflection carries an isosceles trapezoid onto itself, its two diagonals are congruent.
S5-F1-Q3.grading_note: The reflection that swaps A with B and D with C sends diagonal AC onto diagonal BD, and reflections keep lengths.

S5-F1-Q4.skill: Use a symmetry to deduce congruent parts of the figure
S5-F1-Q4.prompt: A reflection carries rectangle ABCD onto itself and swaps vertices A and B (and C and D). Which equality follows?
S5-F1-Q4.grading_note: The reflection sends side AD onto side BC.

S5-F1-Q5.skill: Use a symmetry to deduce congruent parts of the figure
S5-F1-Q5.prompt: If a 180° rotation about a point carries a quadrilateral onto itself, the quadrilateral must be a rectangle.
S5-F1-Q5.grading_note: Every parallelogram has 180° rotation symmetry; most are not rectangles.

S5-F2-Q1.skill: Combine symmetries and identify a figure from its symmetries
S5-F2-Q1.prompt: Rectangle ABCD (not a square) has center O. Reflect it across the line through the midpoints of AB and CD, then across the line through the midpoints of BC and DA. Which single transformation has the same result?
S5-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Reflections across perpendicular lines through O combine to a 180° rotation about O.

S5-F2-Q2.skill: Combine symmetries and identify a figure from its symmetries
S5-F2-Q2.prompt: A quadrilateral is carried onto itself by exactly two transformations: the 360° rotation and one reflection across a line through two of its vertices. Which could it be?
choices: A parallelogram that is not a rectangle or a rhombus
A rectangle that is not a square
A kite that is not a rhombus
S5-F2-Q2.correct_answer: A kite that is not a rhombus
S5-F2-Q2.grading_note: A kite has one line of symmetry, through two opposite vertices. A rectangle has two lines and a 180° turn; a general parallelogram has a 180° turn and no line; a square has eight symmetries.

S5-F2-Q3.skill: Combine symmetries and identify a figure from its symmetries
S5-F2-Q3.prompt: A quadrilateral that is carried onto itself by a 180° rotation about a point must be a rectangle.
S5-F2-Q3.grading_note: Every parallelogram has 180° rotation symmetry about the crossing point of its diagonals.

S5-F2-Q4.skill: Combine symmetries and identify a figure from its symmetries
S5-F2-Q4.prompt: A quadrilateral is carried onto itself by a 180° rotation but by no reflection. What is the most specific name for it?
S5-F2-Q4.correct_answer: A parallelogram that is not a rectangle or a rhombus.
S5-F2-Q4.grading_note: Any equivalent answer. A rectangle or a rhombus would also have reflection symmetries.

S5-F2-Q5.skill: Combine symmetries and identify a figure from its symmetries
S5-F2-Q5.prompt: Doing the same reflection twice gives the same result as the 360° rotation (the identity).
S5-F2-Q5.grading_note: Each point goes to its image and back again.

S6-M-Q1.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a regular polygon onto itself
S6-M-Q1.prompt: Describe every rotation about its center, with angle greater than 0° and at most 360°, that carries a regular pentagon onto itself.
S6-M-Q1.grading_note: Form required: all five angles. Each is a multiple of 360° ÷ 5 = 72°.

S6-M-Q2.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a regular polygon onto itself
S6-M-Q2.prompt: How many reflections carry a regular hexagon onto itself? Describe their lines.
S6-M-Q2.correct_answer: 6 reflections: 3 across lines through pairs of opposite vertices and 3 across lines through the midpoints of pairs of opposite sides.
S6-M-Q2.grading_note: Form required: the number and both kinds of lines.

S6-M-Q3.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a regular polygon onto itself
S6-M-Q3.prompt: Which rotation about its center carries a regular octagon onto itself?

S6-M-Q4.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a regular polygon onto itself
S6-M-Q4.prompt: Each line of symmetry of a regular nonagon (9 sides) passes through one vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.
S6-M-Q4.grading_note: A regular polygon with an odd number of sides has n lines of symmetry, each through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.

S6-M-Q5.skill: Rotations and reflections that carry a regular polygon onto itself
S6-M-Q5.prompt: Describe every reflection that carries an equilateral triangle onto itself.
S6-M-Q5.correct_answer: 3 reflections: across each line through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.
S6-M-Q5.grading_note: Form required: the number and the lines.

S6-B1-Q1.skill: Find the angle of a fraction of a full turn
S6-B1-Q1.prompt: How many degrees are in {1/5} of a full turn?

S6-B1-Q2.skill: Find the angle of a fraction of a full turn
S6-B1-Q2.prompt: How many degrees are in {1/8} of a full turn?

S6-B1-Q3.skill: Find the angle of a fraction of a full turn
S6-B1-Q3.prompt: How many degrees are in {3/6} of a full turn?
S6-B1-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 3/6 = 1/2 and 1/2 of 360 is 180.

S6-B1-Q4.skill: Find the angle of a fraction of a full turn

S6-B1-Q5.skill: Find the angle of a fraction of a full turn

choices: A rhombus that is not a square
A rectangle that is not a square
S6-B2-Q1.grading_note: A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal.

S6-B2-Q2.prompt: A polygon with all sides equal must be regular.
S6-B2-Q2.grading_note: A rhombus that is not a square has equal sides but unequal angles.

S6-B2-Q3.prompt: How many sides does a regular decagon have?

S6-B2-Q4.prompt: What is the name of the regular polygon with 4 sides?

S6-B2-Q5.prompt: A regular hexagon has 6 equal angles.
S6-B2-Q5.grading_note: Regular means all sides and all angles are equal.

S6-B3-Q1.skill: Find lines of symmetry of regular polygons
S6-B3-Q1.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?

S6-B3-Q2.skill: Find lines of symmetry of regular polygons
S6-B3-Q2.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?

S6-B3-Q3.skill: Find lines of symmetry of regular polygons
S6-B3-Q3.prompt: Every line of symmetry of a regular polygon passes through its center.
S6-B3-Q3.grading_note: A reflection that carries the polygon onto itself keeps its center fixed, so the center is on the line.

S6-B3-Q4.skill: Find lines of symmetry of regular polygons
S6-B3-Q4.prompt: A line of symmetry of a square passes through
choices: exactly one vertex and no midpoint
two opposite vertices, or the midpoints of two opposite sides
S6-B3-Q4.correct_answer: two opposite vertices, or the midpoints of two opposite sides
S6-B3-Q4.grading_note: A square has 2 diagonal lines and 2 lines through midpoints of opposite sides.

S6-B3-Q5.skill: Find lines of symmetry of regular polygons
S6-B3-Q5.prompt: A regular hexagon has exactly 3 lines of symmetry.
S6-B3-Q5.grading_note: It has 6: 3 through opposite vertices and 3 through midpoints of opposite sides.

S6-F1-Q1.skill: Work backward from a symmetry to the regular polygon
S6-F1-Q1.prompt: The smallest positive rotation that carries a regular polygon onto itself is 24°. How many sides does it have?

S6-F1-Q2.skill: Work backward from a symmetry to the regular polygon
S6-F1-Q2.prompt: A regular polygon has 20 lines of symmetry. What is the smallest positive rotation that carries it onto itself?
S6-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form. A regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry, so n = 20 and 360 ÷ 20 = 18.

S6-F1-Q3.skill: Work backward from a symmetry to the regular polygon
S6-F1-Q3.prompt: A regular polygon can have 50° as its smallest positive rotation onto itself.
S6-F1-Q3.grading_note: 360 ÷ 50 = 7.2 is not a whole number of sides.

S6-F1-Q4.skill: Work backward from a symmetry to the regular polygon
S6-F1-Q4.prompt: Which can be the smallest positive rotation that carries a regular polygon onto itself?
S6-F1-Q4.grading_note: The angle must be 360° ÷ n for a whole number n ≥ 3; 360 ÷ 40 = 9.

S6-F1-Q5.skill: Work backward from a symmetry to the regular polygon
S6-F1-Q5.prompt: Counting the 360° rotation, how many rotations and reflections in all carry a regular 12-gon onto itself?
S6-F1-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 12 rotations (30°, 60°, ..., 360°) and 12 reflections.

S6-F2-Q1.skill: Combine symmetries of a regular polygon
S6-F2-Q1.prompt: Regular hexagon ABCDEF is labeled counterclockwise. It is rotated 120° counterclockwise about its center. Which vertex position does A move to?
S6-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Each 60° turn moves a vertex one place counterclockwise.

S6-F2-Q2.skill: Combine symmetries of a regular polygon
S6-F2-Q2.prompt: Regular hexagon ABCDEF is labeled counterclockwise. Rotate it 60° counterclockwise about its center, then reflect it across line AD (through the original positions of A and D). Which original vertex position does vertex B end at?
S6-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. The rotation moves B to the position of C; the reflection across AD swaps C and E.

S6-F2-Q3.skill: Combine symmetries of a regular polygon
S6-F2-Q3.prompt: For a regular pentagon, a reflection followed by a different reflection that carries it onto itself is a rotation that carries it onto itself.
S6-F2-Q3.grading_note: Two reflections across lines through the center combine into a rotation about the center.

S6-F2-Q4.skill: Combine symmetries of a regular polygon
S6-F2-Q4.prompt: Square ABCD is labeled counterclockwise. Reflect it across line AC, then rotate it 90° counterclockwise about its center. Which original vertex position does vertex B end at?
S6-F2-Q4.grading_note: The reflection across AC sends B to the position of D; the 90° turn moves D to the position of A.

S6-F2-Q5.skill: Combine symmetries of a regular polygon
S6-F2-Q5.prompt: Two successive 72° rotations of a regular pentagon about its center equal which single transformation?
S6-F2-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Rotation angles about the same center add.

S7-M-Q1.prompt: Complete a precise definition. A reflection across line ℓ maps each point P not on ℓ to the point P′ such that ______. Each point on ℓ maps to ______.
S7-M-Q1.correct_answer: ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of segment PP′; itself.
S7-M-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Both blanks are needed. "P′ is the same distance from ℓ" alone is not enough: it must be on the perpendicular through P, on the other side.

S7-M-Q2.prompt: Points A and B are different. Write a precise definition of the translation that maps A to B.
S7-M-Q2.correct_answer: It maps each point P to the point P′ such that PP′ has the same length as AB, is parallel to AB (or on line AB), and points in the same direction.
S7-M-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: same length, parallel (or collinear), same direction. Accept "ABP′P is a parallelogram" for points P not on line AB.

S7-M-Q3.prompt: Point P′ is the image of point P under a reflection across line ℓ, and P is not on ℓ. Which must be true?
choices: ℓ is perpendicular to PP′ and passes through its midpoint
P and P′ are on the same side of ℓ
S7-M-Q3.correct_answer: ℓ is perpendicular to PP′ and passes through its midpoint
S7-M-Q3.grading_note: By the definition of a reflection, ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP′.

figure.desc: A horizontal line ℓ. Point P is above it and point P′ is directly below it; a dashed segment joins P and P′.

S7-M-Q4.prompt: Under a translation, all the segments that join points to their images are parallel (or on one line) and have the same length.
S7-M-Q4.grading_note: That is what the definition of a translation says about every point.

S7-M-Q5.prompt: A reflection maps P(1, 2) to P′(5, 2). Use the definition to find the line of reflection.
S7-M-Q5.grading_note: Form required: an equation of the line. The line is the perpendicular bisector of PP′: PP′ is horizontal with midpoint (3, 2), so the line is the vertical line x = 3.

S7-B1-Q1.skill: Find the midpoint of a horizontal or vertical segment
S7-B1-Q1.prompt: Find the midpoint of the segment from (2, 4) to (8, 4).
S7-B1-Q1.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. Halfway from x = 2 to x = 8 is x = 5.

S7-B2-Q1.prompt: A horizontal segment and a vertical segment are perpendicular.
S7-B2-Q1.grading_note: Horizontal and vertical directions meet at right angles.

S7-B2-Q4.correct_answer: Any horizontal segment through (5, 3), for example from (4, 3) to (8, 3).

S7-B2-Q5.prompt: Which describes two lines that are both perpendicular to the x-axis?
choices: They are perpendicular to each other
S7-B2-Q5.grading_note: Both are vertical lines, so they are parallel (or the same line if they have the same x-value).

S7-F1-Q1.skill: Find lines of reflection and images in slanted, non-axis cases
S7-F1-Q1.prompt: A reflection maps P(0, 0) to P′(4, 2). Find an equation of the line of reflection.
S7-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent equation. The midpoint of PP′ is (2, 1); PP′ has slope 1/2, so the perpendicular bisector has slope -2: y - 1 = -2(x - 2).

S7-F1-Q2.skill: Find lines of reflection and images in slanted, non-axis cases
S7-F1-Q2.prompt: A translation maps A(2, -1) to A′(-3, 4). Where does it map B(0, 6)?
S7-F1-Q2.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. The translation moves every point 5 left and 5 up.

S7-F1-Q3.skill: Find lines of reflection and images in slanted, non-axis cases
S7-F1-Q3.prompt: A reflection maps P to P′ and Q to Q′, where P and Q are not on the line of reflection. Then PP′ is parallel to QQ′ (or on the same line).
S7-F1-Q3.grading_note: Both segments are perpendicular to the line of reflection.

S7-F1-Q4.skill: Find lines of reflection and images in slanted, non-axis cases
S7-F1-Q4.prompt: A reflection maps A(1, 3) to A′(3, 1). Is the line of reflection y = x? Use the definition to decide.
S7-F1-Q4.correct_answer: Yes. The midpoint (2, 2) is on y = x, and AA′ (slope -1) is perpendicular to y = x (slope 1).
S7-F1-Q4.grading_note: Form required: the conclusion with both conditions of the definition checked (midpoint and perpendicularity).

S7-F1-Q5.skill: Find lines of reflection and images in slanted, non-axis cases
S7-F1-Q5.prompt: A reflection maps P(-1, 4) to P′(5, 4). Which point is on the line of reflection?
S7-F1-Q5.grading_note: The line is x = 2, the vertical perpendicular bisector of the horizontal segment PP′.

S7-F2-Q1.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
S7-F2-Q1.prompt: Points P and Q are on the same side of line ℓ, and line PQ is not perpendicular to ℓ. A reflection across ℓ maps them to P′ and Q′. Let PP′ meet ℓ at M and QQ′ meet ℓ at N. Prove that PQ = P′Q′.
S7-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: PM = P′M and QN = Q′N with right angles at M and N (definition); triangles PMN and P′MN are congruent by SAS, so PN = P′N and ∠PNM ≅ ∠P′NM; subtracting from the right angles gives ∠PNQ ≅ ∠P′NQ′; then triangles PNQ and P′NQ′ are congruent by SAS, so PQ = P′Q′. Alternative: coordinates with ℓ as the x-axis. Invalid: "reflections preserve distance" (that is what is being proved).
S7-F2-Q1.required_method: Use the definition (ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP′ and of QQ′), then two pairs of congruent triangles (SAS): PMN ≅ P′MN, then PNQ ≅ P′NQ′.

S7-F2-Q2.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
S7-F2-Q2.prompt: A translation maps P to P′ and Q to Q′, where Q is not on line PP′. Prove that PQ = P′Q′.
S7-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: PP′ ∥ QQ′ and PP′ = QQ′ in the same direction, so PP′Q′Q is a parallelogram (one pair of opposite sides parallel and congruent); opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent, so PQ = P′Q′. Invalid: assuming translations preserve length.
S7-F2-Q2.required_method: Use the definition (PP′ and QQ′ are parallel, the same length, and the same direction) to show PP′Q′Q is a parallelogram.

S7-F2-Q3.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
S7-F2-Q3.prompt: A translation maps P to P′ and Q to Q′. Then PP′Q′Q is always a parallelogram.
S7-F2-Q3.grading_note: If Q is on line PP′, all four points lie on one line, so there is no parallelogram.

S7-F2-Q4.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
S7-F2-Q4.prompt: Under a reflection, a point not on the line of reflection and its image are on the same side of the line.
S7-F2-Q4.grading_note: They are on opposite sides; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.

S7-F2-Q5.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
S7-F2-Q5.prompt: In a proof that a reflection across ℓ keeps the length of segment PQ, which fact is used first?
choices: ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP′ and of QQ′
S7-F2-Q5.correct_answer: ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP′ and of QQ′
S7-F2-Q5.grading_note: The proof starts from the definition of a reflection.

S8-M-Q1.prompt: Complete a precise definition. A counterclockwise rotation about point O through angle θ maps each point P ≠ O to the point P′ such that ______ and ______. Point O maps to ______.
S8-M-Q1.correct_answer: OP′ = OP (P′ is on the circle with center O through P); m∠POP′ = θ, measured counterclockwise from ray OP; itself.
S8-M-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. All three blanks are needed.

S8-M-Q2.prompt: A rotation about point O maps point P to P′ (P ≠ P′). Which must be true?
choices: O is the midpoint of PP′
O is on the perpendicular bisector of PP′
S8-M-Q2.correct_answer: O is on the perpendicular bisector of PP′
S8-M-Q2.grading_note: OP = OP′, so O is equidistant from P and P′ and lies on the perpendicular bisector of PP′. O is the midpoint only for a 180° rotation.

S8-M-Q3.prompt: A rotation of 90° counterclockwise about O(1, 1) maps P(4, 1) to P′. Use the definition to find P′.
S8-M-Q3.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. P is 3 units right of O; after a 90° counterclockwise turn it is 3 units above O.

figure.desc: Coordinate grid from -1 to 6 with points O(1, 1) and P(4, 1).

S8-M-Q4.prompt: Under a rotation about point O, each point P moves along the circle with center O that passes through P.

S8-M-Q5.prompt: A rotation maps P(2, 0) to P′(0, 2). Explain why its center must lie on the line y = x.
S8-M-Q5.correct_answer: The center is the same distance from P and from P′, so it is on the perpendicular bisector of PP′. That bisector passes through (1, 1) with slope 1, which is the line y = x.
S8-M-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that uses equal distances from the center (the definition) and the perpendicular bisector.
