S9-B2-Q5.skill: Find image points with coordinate rules
S9-B2-Q5.prompt: The image of (2, 2) under a 180° rotation about the origin is (2, -2).

S9-B3-Q1.skill: Count the distance from a point to a horizontal or vertical line
S9-B3-Q1.prompt: How far is the point (5, 3) from the vertical line x = 1?

S9-B3-Q2.skill: Count the distance from a point to a horizontal or vertical line
S9-B3-Q2.prompt: How far is the point (-2, -1) from the horizontal line y = 3?

S9-B3-Q3.skill: Count the distance from a point to a horizontal or vertical line
S9-B3-Q3.prompt: Which point is 3 units from the line x = 2, on its left?

S9-B3-Q4.skill: Count the distance from a point to a horizontal or vertical line
S9-B3-Q4.prompt: The point (0, 4) is 4 units from the x-axis.

S9-B3-Q5.skill: Count the distance from a point to a horizontal or vertical line
S9-B3-Q5.prompt: The point (6, 2) is 6 units from the line x = 2.

S9-F1-Q1.skill: Draw the image under a sequence of two transformations
S9-F1-Q1.prompt: Reflect triangle ABC across the y-axis, then translate the result 3 units down. Draw and label the final image A″B″C″.
S9-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any drawing with these vertices (within about a quarter of a grid square), joined in order and labeled. (x, y) → (-x, y) → (-x, y - 3).

figure.desc: Coordinate grid from -6 to 6 with triangle ABC: A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(2, 5).

S9-F1-Q2.skill: Draw the image under a sequence of two transformations
S9-F1-Q2.prompt: Rotate triangle ABC by 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then reflect the result across the x-axis. Draw and label the final image A″B″C″.
S9-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any drawing with these vertices (within about a quarter of a grid square), joined in order and labeled. (x, y) → (-y, x) → (-y, -x).

figure.desc: Coordinate grid from -6 to 6 with triangle ABC: A(1, 1), B(3, 1), C(3, 4).

S9-F1-Q3.skill: Draw the image under a sequence of two transformations
S9-F1-Q3.prompt: Triangle ABC has A(2, 1). It is translated 2 units right and then rotated 180° about the origin. Where does A end up?

S9-F1-Q4.skill: Draw the image under a sequence of two transformations
S9-F1-Q4.prompt: Reflecting a figure across the x-axis and then across the y-axis gives the same image as reflecting it across the line y = x.
S9-F1-Q4.grading_note: The two reflections give (x, y) → (-x, -y), a 180° rotation; reflecting across y = x gives (y, x).

S9-F1-Q5.skill: Draw the image under a sequence of two transformations
S9-F1-Q5.prompt: Point P(1, 3) is translated 2 units left and then reflected across the line y = x. Where does it end up?

S9-F2-Q1.skill: Draw rotations and reflections off the grid with compass, protractor, and straightedge
S9-F2-Q1.prompt: Use a compass and protractor. Rotate point P 60° counterclockwise about point O. Mark and label the image P′.
S9-F2-Q1.correct_answer: P′ is on the circle with center O through P, with m∠POP′ = 60° measured counterclockwise from ray OP.
S9-F2-Q1.grading_note: Accept within about 2° and 2 mm. Evidence: the arc (or equal compass distance) from O and the 60° angle.

figure.desc: Two points on a blank page: center O and point P to its right, a little above.

S9-F2-Q2.skill: Draw rotations and reflections off the grid with compass, protractor, and straightedge
S9-F2-Q2.prompt: Use a compass and straightedge. Reflect point Q across line ℓ. Mark and label the image Q′.
S9-F2-Q2.correct_answer: Q′ is on the perpendicular from Q to ℓ, on the other side of ℓ, the same distance from ℓ as Q (ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of QQ′).
S9-F2-Q2.grading_note: Accept within about 2 mm. Evidence: the construction of the perpendicular from Q to ℓ and equal distances.

figure.desc: A slanted line ℓ rising to the right, and point Q above it.

S9-F2-Q3.skill: Draw rotations and reflections off the grid with compass, protractor, and straightedge
S9-F2-Q3.prompt: Use a compass and protractor. Rotate segment AB 90° clockwise about point A. Draw and label the image AB′.
S9-F2-Q3.correct_answer: AB′ has the same length as AB, with m∠BAB′ = 90° measured clockwise from ray AB; A stays fixed.
S9-F2-Q3.grading_note: Accept within about 2° and 2 mm. Evidence: equal lengths and the 90° angle.

figure.desc: Segment AB on a blank page, rising to the right from A.

S9-F2-Q4.skill: Draw rotations and reflections off the grid with compass, protractor, and straightedge
S9-F2-Q4.prompt: To rotate point P about point O by 45°, it is enough to draw a 45° angle at O; the distance from O does not matter.
S9-F2-Q4.grading_note: The image must also be the same distance from O as P (on the circle centered at O through P).

S9-F2-Q5.skill: Draw rotations and reflections off the grid with compass, protractor, and straightedge
S9-F2-Q5.prompt: Describe how to reflect point P across a slanted line ℓ using only a compass and straightedge.
S9-F2-Q5.correct_answer: Construct the line through P perpendicular to ℓ; mark where it meets ℓ (M); with the compass set to MP, mark the point P′ on that perpendicular, on the other side of ℓ, so that MP′ = MP.
S9-F2-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent construction (for example, two circles centered at two points of ℓ through P meet again at P′).

S10-M-Q1.skill: Specify a sequence of transformations that carries one figure onto another
S10-M-Q1.prompt: Describe a sequence of rigid transformations that carries triangle ABC onto triangle A′B′C′ (A to A′, B to B′, C to C′).
S10-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid sequence, for example a reflection across the x-axis followed by a reflection across the y-axis. Check: every vertex must land on its partner.

figure.desc: Grid from -5 to 5. Triangle ABC: A(1, 1), B(3, 1), C(1, 4). Triangle A′B′C′: A′(-1, -1), B′(-3, -1), C′(-1, -4).

S10-M-Q2.skill: Specify a sequence of transformations that carries one figure onto another
S10-M-Q2.prompt: Describe a sequence of rigid transformations that carries triangle ABC onto triangle A′B′C′.
S10-M-Q2.correct_answer: Reflect across the x-axis, then translate 3 units left.
S10-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid sequence (for example, translate 3 units left, then reflect across the x-axis). The orientation is reversed, so the sequence must include a reflection.

figure.desc: Grid from -6 to 6. Triangle ABC: A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(2, 5). Triangle A′B′C′: A′(-2, -2), B′(1, -2), C′(-1, -5).

S10-M-Q3.skill: Specify a sequence of transformations that carries one figure onto another
S10-M-Q3.prompt: On the grid, triangle A′B′C′ is congruent to triangle ABC. Describe a sequence of rigid transformations that carries ABC onto A′B′C′, with A → A′, B → B′, C → C′.
S10-M-Q3.correct_answer: Rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 1 unit up.
S10-M-Q3.grading_note: Any valid sequence. Check: (x, y) → (-y, x) → (-y, x + 1) sends A(2, 1) to (-1, 3), B to (-1, 6), C to (-3, 3).

figure.desc: Grid from -6 to 6. Triangle ABC: A(2, 1), B(5, 1), C(2, 3). Triangle A′B′C′: A′(-1, 3), B′(-1, 6), C′(-3, 3).

S10-M-Q4.skill: Specify a sequence of transformations that carries one figure onto another
S10-M-Q4.prompt: Right triangle ABC has A(0, 0), B(2, 0), C(0, 3). Triangle A′B′C′ has A′(4, 0), B′(4, 2), C′(1, 0). Which sequence carries ABC onto A′B′C′?
choices: Reflect across the y-axis, then translate 4 units right
Rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 4 units right
Rotate 90° clockwise about the origin, then translate 4 units right
Translate 4 units right, then rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin
S10-M-Q4.correct_answer: Rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 4 units right
S10-M-Q4.grading_note: The rotation sends B to (0, 2) and C to (-3, 0); the translation then gives B′(4, 2) and C′(1, 0). The other orders or turns send B or C elsewhere.

S10-M-Q5.skill: Specify a sequence of transformations that carries one figure onto another
S10-M-Q5.prompt: Triangles PQR and P′Q′R′ are congruent. P, Q, R are in clockwise order and P′, Q′, R′ are in counterclockwise order. Some sequence of rotations and translations alone carries P to P′, Q to Q′, and R to R′.
S10-M-Q5.grading_note: Rotations and translations keep the order (orientation) of the vertices; a reflection is needed to reverse it.

S10-B1-Q1.skill: Understand congruence as the result of one rigid motion
S10-B1-Q1.prompt: Triangle 2 is the image of triangle 1 after one rigid motion. Every point moved 3 units right. Which motion was it?
S10-B1-Q1.grading_note: Sliding every point the same way is a translation.

S10-B1-Q2.skill: Understand congruence as the result of one rigid motion
S10-B1-Q2.prompt: A triangle and its image face opposite ways, as in a mirror. Which kind of rigid motion was most likely used?

S10-B1-Q3.skill: Understand congruence as the result of one rigid motion
S10-B1-Q3.prompt: If one figure is the image of another under a sequence of rigid motions, the figures are congruent.
S10-B1-Q3.grading_note: Rigid motions keep all lengths and angles.

S10-B1-Q4.skill: Understand congruence as the result of one rigid motion
S10-B1-Q4.prompt: A figure and its image under a rigid motion can have different areas.

S10-B1-Q5.skill: Understand congruence as the result of one rigid motion
S10-B1-Q5.prompt: Segment AB goes from (0, 0) to (2, 0). Its image goes from (0, 0) to (0, 2). Which single rigid motion could do this?
choices: A 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin
S10-B1-Q5.correct_answer: A 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin
S10-B1-Q5.grading_note: (2, 0) → (0, 2) under (x, y) → (-y, x), and the origin stays fixed.

S10-B2-Q1.skill: Find images with coordinate rules for sequences
S10-B2-Q1.prompt: Point (2, -3) is reflected across the y-axis. Find its image.

S10-B2-Q2.skill: Find images with coordinate rules for sequences
S10-B2-Q2.prompt: Point (-1, 4) is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin. Find its image.
S10-B2-Q2.grading_note: Form required: an ordered pair. (x, y) → (-y, x).

S10-B2-Q3.skill: Find images with coordinate rules for sequences
S10-B2-Q3.prompt: Point (5, 1) is translated 2 units left and 3 units down. Find its image.

S10-B2-Q4.skill: Find images with coordinate rules for sequences
S10-B2-Q4.prompt: Point (0, 3) rotated 180° about the origin is (0, -3).

S10-B2-Q5.skill: Find images with coordinate rules for sequences
S10-B2-Q5.prompt: Point (4, 1) reflected across the line y = x is (4, -1).

S10-B3-Q1.skill: Read the orientation (clockwise or counterclockwise order) of a triangle
S10-B3-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC has A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(0, 3). Going A → B → C, is the order clockwise or counterclockwise?
S10-B3-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. From A go right to B, then up-left to C: a counterclockwise turn.

S10-B3-Q2.skill: Read the orientation (clockwise or counterclockwise order) of a triangle
S10-B3-Q2.prompt: A reflection reverses the orientation of a triangle.
S10-B3-Q2.grading_note: A mirror image runs the other way around.

S10-B3-Q3.skill: Read the orientation (clockwise or counterclockwise order) of a triangle
S10-B3-Q3.prompt: A rotation reverses the orientation of a triangle.
S10-B3-Q3.grading_note: Rotations keep the order of the vertices.

S10-B3-Q4.skill: Read the orientation (clockwise or counterclockwise order) of a triangle
S10-B3-Q4.prompt: Triangle PQR is clockwise. After two reflections, its image is
S10-B3-Q4.grading_note: Each reflection reverses the order, so two reflections restore it.

S10-B3-Q5.skill: Read the orientation (clockwise or counterclockwise order) of a triangle
S10-B3-Q5.prompt: Triangle ABC is counterclockwise. It is translated and then reflected. Is the final image clockwise or counterclockwise?
S10-B3-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. The translation keeps the order; the reflection reverses it.

S10-F1-Q1.skill: Use the fewest transformations and justify
S10-F1-Q1.prompt: Two reflections are done one after the other, across parallel lines that are 3 units apart. Which single transformation has the same result?
S10-F1-Q1.correct_answer: A translation of 6 units, perpendicular to the lines (in the direction from the first line toward the second).
S10-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent wording with the distance (twice the gap) and the direction.

S10-F1-Q2.skill: Use the fewest transformations and justify
S10-F1-Q2.prompt: Two reflections are done one after the other, across lines that meet at point O and form a 40° angle. Which single transformation has the same result?
S10-F1-Q2.correct_answer: A rotation of 80° about O (in the direction from the first line toward the second).
S10-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent wording with the center and twice the angle.

S10-F1-Q3.skill: Use the fewest transformations and justify
S10-F1-Q3.prompt: Triangle ABC is clockwise and triangle A′B′C′ is congruent to it and counterclockwise. Explain why no single rotation or translation carries ABC onto A′B′C′.
S10-F1-Q3.correct_answer: Rotations and translations keep orientation, but these triangles have opposite orientations, so a reflection is needed.
S10-F1-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation based on orientation.

S10-F1-Q4.skill: Use the fewest transformations and justify
S10-F1-Q4.prompt: Every rigid motion of the plane can be written as a sequence of at most three reflections.
S10-F1-Q4.grading_note: This is a known theorem: a reflection fixes one vertex, a second fixes two, and a third (if needed) fixes the third vertex of a triangle.

S10-F1-Q5.skill: Use the fewest transformations and justify
S10-F1-Q5.prompt: Triangle A′B′C′ is the image of triangle ABC under some rigid motion, and both are counterclockwise. What is the fewest number of reflections that can always carry ABC onto A′B′C′?
S10-F1-Q5.grading_note: The orientation is kept, so an even number is needed; two reflections give any rotation or translation.

S10-F2-Q1.skill: Specify a similarity sequence: a dilation and rigid motions
S10-F2-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC has A(0, 0), B(2, 0), C(0, 1). Triangle A′B′C′ has A′(0, 0), B′(0, 6), C′(-3, 0). Describe a sequence (a dilation and a rigid motion) that carries ABC onto A′B′C′.
S10-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Dilate by a factor of 3 about the origin, then rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin.

S10-F2-Q2.skill: Specify a similarity sequence: a dilation and rigid motions
S10-F2-Q2.prompt: Square S has vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1). Square T has vertices (2, 2), (4, 2), (4, 4), (2, 4). Describe a similarity sequence carrying S onto T.
S10-F2-Q2.correct_answer: Dilate by 2 about the origin, then translate 2 units right and 2 units up.

S10-F2-Q3.skill: Specify a similarity sequence: a dilation and rigid motions
S10-F2-Q3.prompt: Any two figures that a sequence of rigid motions and a dilation carries one onto the other are congruent.
S10-F2-Q3.grading_note: They are similar; they are congruent only when the scale factor is 1.

S10-F2-Q4.skill: Specify a similarity sequence: a dilation and rigid motions
S10-F2-Q4.prompt: Segment AB is from (0, 0) to (3, 0). Segment CD is from (1, 1) to (1, 7). Which sequence carries AB onto CD (A to C, B to D)?
choices: Rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 1 right and 1 up
Dilate by 2 about the origin, then translate 1 right and 1 up
Dilate by 3 about the origin, rotate 90° counterclockwise, then translate 1 right and 1 up
Dilate by 2 about the origin, rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 1 right and 1 up
S10-F2-Q4.correct_answer: Dilate by 2 about the origin, rotate 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 1 right and 1 up

S10-F2-Q5.skill: Specify a similarity sequence: a dilation and rigid motions
S10-F2-Q5.prompt: Triangle PQR has sides 3, 4, 5. Triangle XYZ has sides 6, 8, 10. What scale factor must the dilation in a similarity sequence from PQR to XYZ have?
S10-F2-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Each side of XYZ is 2 times the matching side of PQR.

S11-M-Q1.skill: Predict the effect of a rigid motion on a figure
S11-M-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC has AB = 7, BC = 5, and m∠B = 48°. It is reflected across a line ℓ. What are A′B′ and m∠B′?
choices: They depend on where ℓ is
S11-M-Q1.grading_note: A reflection is a rigid motion: it keeps every length and every angle measure, wherever ℓ is.

S11-M-Q2.skill: Predict the effect of a rigid motion on a figure
S11-M-Q2.prompt: Quadrilateral PQRS has PQ ∥ SR. It is rotated 90° about a point O. What is true about P′Q′ and S′R′? Explain.
S11-M-Q2.correct_answer: P′Q′ ∥ S′R′. A rotation maps lines to lines and keeps them from meeting if they did not meet before, so parallel lines stay parallel.
S11-M-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation. Essential: the images are parallel because rigid motions take parallel lines to parallel lines.

S11-M-Q3.skill: Predict the effect of a rigid motion on a figure
S11-M-Q3.prompt: Point A is 4 cm from line m. Triangle ABC is reflected across m. How far is A′ from m, and on which side of m is it?
S11-M-Q3.correct_answer: 4 cm, on the other side of m.
S11-M-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. m is the perpendicular bisector of AA′.

S11-M-Q4.skill: Predict the effect of a rigid motion on a figure
S11-M-Q4.prompt: A translation can reverse the orientation (the clockwise or counterclockwise order) of a triangle's vertices.
S11-M-Q4.grading_note: A translation slides every point the same way, so the order of the vertices around the triangle is kept.

S11-M-Q5.skill: Predict the effect of a rigid motion on a figure
S11-M-Q5.prompt: Segment AB lies on line ℓ. A 180° rotation about a point O on ℓ maps AB to A′B′. Where does A′B′ lie? Explain.
S11-M-Q5.correct_answer: On ℓ. A 180° rotation about a point of ℓ sends every point of ℓ to the point of ℓ on the opposite side of O, so ℓ maps onto itself.

S11-B1-Q1.skill: Know what rigid motions keep: lines, lengths, angles, and parallel lines
S11-B1-Q1.prompt: Under a rotation, the image of a line is a line.
S11-B1-Q1.grading_note: Rigid motions map lines to lines.

S11-B1-Q2.skill: Know what rigid motions keep: lines, lengths, angles, and parallel lines
S11-B1-Q2.prompt: A reflection can turn two parallel lines into two lines that meet.
S11-B1-Q2.grading_note: Rigid motions keep parallel lines parallel.

S11-B1-Q3.skill: Know what rigid motions keep: lines, lengths, angles, and parallel lines
S11-B1-Q3.prompt: A 52° angle is translated 6 units to the right. What is the measure of its image?

S11-B1-Q4.skill: Know what rigid motions keep: lines, lengths, angles, and parallel lines
S11-B1-Q4.prompt: A 9 cm segment is rotated 30° about one of its endpoints. How long is its image?

S11-B1-Q5.skill: Know what rigid motions keep: lines, lengths, angles, and parallel lines
S11-B1-Q5.prompt: Name two properties of a figure that a reflection does NOT change.
S11-B1-Q5.correct_answer: Any two of: side lengths, angle measures, area, parallel sides, perimeter.

S11-B2-Q1.skill: Match the vertices and sides of a figure with its image
S11-B2-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC is rotated to triangle A′B′C′. Which side of the image corresponds to side BC?

S11-B2-Q2.skill: Match the vertices and sides of a figure with its image
S11-B2-Q2.prompt: Quadrilateral PQRS is reflected to P′Q′R′S′. Which angle corresponds to ∠Q?
S11-B2-Q2.grading_note: The prime marks the image of each vertex.

S11-B2-Q3.skill: Match the vertices and sides of a figure with its image
S11-B2-Q3.prompt: If triangle ABC is translated to triangle A′B′C′, then AB = A′B′.
S11-B2-Q3.grading_note: Corresponding sides of an image under a rigid motion are equal.

S11-B2-Q4.skill: Match the vertices and sides of a figure with its image
S11-B2-Q4.prompt: Triangle DEF is reflected to D′E′F′. DE = 6 and EF = 9. Find D′E′ and E′F′.

S11-B2-Q5.skill: Match the vertices and sides of a figure with its image
S11-B2-Q5.prompt: After a rotation, side A′B′ of the image always lies on top of side AB.
S11-B2-Q5.grading_note: The image is usually in a new position; it only has the same length.

S11-F1-Q1.skill: Predict the effect of a sequence of rigid motions
S11-F1-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC is reflected across line ℓ and then across line m, where ℓ ∥ m. Is the final image clockwise or counterclockwise if ABC is counterclockwise? Explain.
S11-F1-Q1.correct_answer: Counterclockwise. Each reflection reverses the orientation, so two reflections restore it.

S11-F1-Q2.skill: Predict the effect of a sequence of rigid motions
S11-F1-Q2.prompt: A figure is rotated 70° about point O and then rotated 50° about the same point O. Which single rigid motion has the same effect?
S11-F1-Q2.correct_answer: A rotation of 120° about O (in the same direction).

S11-F1-Q3.skill: Predict the effect of a sequence of rigid motions
S11-F1-Q3.prompt: A translation that is not the identity has exactly one fixed point.
S11-F1-Q3.grading_note: Every point moves by the same nonzero amount, so no point is fixed.

S11-F1-Q4.skill: Predict the effect of a sequence of rigid motions
S11-F1-Q4.prompt: Which rigid motion keeps exactly one point fixed?
choices: A rotation of 90° about point O
S11-F1-Q4.correct_answer: A rotation of 90° about point O
S11-F1-Q4.grading_note: A 90° rotation fixes only its center; a reflection fixes every point of its line; a translation fixes none.

S11-F1-Q5.skill: Predict the effect of a sequence of rigid motions
S11-F1-Q5.prompt: Line ℓ is reflected across line m, and ℓ is perpendicular to m. What is the image of ℓ? Explain.
S11-F1-Q5.correct_answer: ℓ itself. Each point of ℓ goes to the point of ℓ on the other side of m, the same distance away.
S11-F1-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation (a line perpendicular to the mirror maps onto itself).

S11-F2-Q1.skill: Use a rigid motion to conclude that parts of a figure are congruent
S11-F2-Q1.prompt: A rotation about O maps triangle OAB onto triangle OCD, with A → C and B → D. OA = 5 and AB = 7. Find OC and CD.
S11-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The rotation sends OA to OC and AB to CD, keeping lengths.

S11-F2-Q2.skill: Use a rigid motion to conclude that parts of a figure are congruent
S11-F2-Q2.prompt: A reflection across line ℓ maps triangle PQR onto triangle PSR (Q → S, and P and R are on ℓ). m∠PQR = 64°. Find m∠PSR.

S11-F2-Q3.skill: Use a rigid motion to conclude that parts of a figure are congruent
S11-F2-Q3.prompt: If a rigid motion maps segment AB onto segment CD, then AB could be longer than CD.
S11-F2-Q3.grading_note: Rigid motions keep lengths, so AB = CD.

S11-F2-Q4.skill: Use a rigid motion to conclude that parts of a figure are congruent
S11-F2-Q4.prompt: A translation maps triangle KLM onto triangle K′L′M′. Which conclusion is NOT justified?
choices: KL ∥ K′L′ or KL is on line K′L′
KL is on the same line as K′L′
S11-F2-Q4.correct_answer: KL is on the same line as K′L′
S11-F2-Q4.grading_note: A translation keeps length and angle and keeps lines parallel to themselves, but the image is usually on a different line.

S11-F2-Q5.skill: Use a rigid motion to conclude that parts of a figure are congruent
S11-F2-Q5.prompt: Explain why the image of an isosceles triangle under any rigid motion is also isosceles.
S11-F2-Q5.correct_answer: The two equal sides map to two sides of the same lengths, so the image has two equal sides.

S12-M-Q1.skill: Decide whether two figures are congruent using rigid motions
S12-M-Q1.prompt: Is triangle ABC congruent to triangle DEF? If so, give a rigid motion that carries ABC onto DEF. If not, explain why.
S12-M-Q1.correct_answer: Yes. The reflection across the y-axis carries A to D, B to E, and C to F.
S12-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid rigid motion or sequence. The conclusion and a motion that works are both required.

figure.desc: Grid from -6 to 6. Triangle ABC: A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 3). Triangle DEF: D(-1, 1), E(-4, 1), F(-1, 3).

S12-M-Q2.skill: Decide whether two figures are congruent using rigid motions
S12-M-Q2.prompt: Is triangle ABC congruent to triangle PQR? If so, give a rigid motion that carries one onto the other. If not, explain why.
S12-M-Q2.correct_answer: No. ABC has legs 3 and 4, but PQR has legs 3 and 5. A rigid motion keeps every length, so none can carry one onto the other.
S12-M-Q2.grading_note: Form required: "No" with a length (or area) that differs. Areas 6 and 7.5 also show it.

figure.desc: Grid from -6 to 6. Triangle ABC: A(0, 0), B(3, 0), C(0, 4). Triangle PQR: P(-5, -1), Q(-2, -1), R(-5, 4).

S12-M-Q3.skill: Decide whether two figures are congruent using rigid motions
S12-M-Q3.prompt: Which fact proves that two figures are NOT congruent?
choices: One has area 12 and the other has area 15
S12-M-Q3.correct_answer: One has area 12 and the other has area 15
S12-M-Q3.grading_note: Rigid motions keep area. Direction and position can be changed by rigid motions.

S12-M-Q4.skill: Decide whether two figures are congruent using rigid motions
S12-M-Q4.prompt: Two figures are congruent if some sequence of rotations, reflections, and translations carries one onto the other.
S12-M-Q4.grading_note: That is the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.

S12-M-Q5.skill: Decide whether two figures are congruent using rigid motions
S12-M-Q5.prompt: Rectangle R is 4 cm wide and 6 cm tall. Rectangle S is 6 cm wide and 4 cm tall. Are they congruent? Give a rigid motion or explain why not.
S12-M-Q5.correct_answer: Yes. A 90° rotation (followed by a translation if needed) carries R onto S.
S12-M-Q5.grading_note: Any valid rigid motion. Both are 4 by 6 rectangles; turning one a quarter turn matches the other.

S12-B1-Q1.skill: Recognize congruent figures as images under rigid motions
S12-B1-Q1.prompt: If one figure is a translation of another, the figures are congruent.
S12-B1-Q1.grading_note: A translation is a rigid motion.

S12-B1-Q2.skill: Recognize congruent figures as images under rigid motions
S12-B1-Q2.prompt: Two figures with the same shape but different sizes are congruent.

S12-B1-Q3.skill: Recognize congruent figures as images under rigid motions

choices: A square and a larger square
A circle of radius 2 and a circle of radius 3
A triangle and a dilation of it by 2
S12-B1-Q3.grading_note: A reflection keeps size and shape.

S12-B1-Q4.skill: Recognize congruent figures as images under rigid motions

S12-B1-Q5.skill: Recognize congruent figures as images under rigid motions
S12-B1-Q5.prompt: Is a figure congruent to its image after a reflection followed by a translation?
S12-B1-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent answer: both are rigid motions.

S12-B2-Q5.skill: Find lengths on a grid with the Pythagorean Theorem
S12-B2-Q5.prompt: The segment from (0, 0) to (3, 3) has length 3.

S12-F1-Q1.skill: Decide congruence for figures given by measurements, including curved figures
S12-F1-Q1.prompt: Circle P has radius 3 and circle Q has radius 3. Explain, using a rigid motion, why they are congruent.
S12-F1-Q1.correct_answer: Translate P's center to Q's center. Every point 3 units from P's center goes to a point 3 units from Q's center, so circle P lands on circle Q.
S12-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation using a translation that matches the centers.

S12-F1-Q2.skill: Decide congruence for figures given by measurements, including curved figures
S12-F1-Q2.prompt: Two quadrilaterals each have sides 5, 5, 5, 5. One is a square and the other has a 60° angle. Are they congruent? Explain.
S12-F1-Q2.correct_answer: No. A rigid motion keeps angle measures, but one has 90° angles and the other a 60° angle.

S12-F1-Q3.skill: Decide congruence for figures given by measurements, including curved figures
S12-F1-Q3.prompt: Two triangles with the same perimeter must be congruent.
S12-F1-Q3.grading_note: A 3-4-5 triangle and a 4-4-4 triangle both have perimeter 12.

S12-F1-Q4.skill: Decide congruence for figures given by measurements, including curved figures
S12-F1-Q4.prompt: Which information is enough to show two segments are congruent?
choices: They both start at the origin
S12-F1-Q4.grading_note: A rigid motion can carry any segment onto any other segment of the same length.

S12-F1-Q5.skill: Decide congruence for figures given by measurements, including curved figures
S12-F1-Q5.prompt: Angle 1 measures 35° and angle 2 measures 35°. Describe a rigid motion that carries angle 1 onto angle 2.
S12-F1-Q5.correct_answer: Translate the vertex of angle 1 to the vertex of angle 2, rotate so one side lies along a side of angle 2, and reflect across that side if the other side is on the wrong side.
S12-F1-Q5.grading_note: Any valid description that matches vertex and both sides.

S12-F2-Q1.skill: Use an established congruence to find unknown parts
S12-F2-Q1.prompt: A rigid motion carries quadrilateral ABCD onto quadrilateral EFGH with A → E, B → F, C → G, D → H. AB = 6, ∠C = 110°, and GH = 4. Find EF, ∠G, and CD.

S12-F2-Q2.skill: Use an established congruence to find unknown parts
S12-F2-Q2.prompt: Triangle RST is congruent to triangle XYZ by a rigid motion with R → X, S → Y, T → Z. RS = 2x + 3 and XY = 15. Find x.
S12-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent form. RS = XY, so 2x + 3 = 15.

S12-F2-Q3.skill: Use an established congruence to find unknown parts
S12-F2-Q3.prompt: If a rigid motion carries triangle ABC onto triangle DEF with A → D, B → E, C → F, then ∠B ≅ ∠F.

S12-F2-Q4.skill: Use an established congruence to find unknown parts
S12-F2-Q4.prompt: A reflection carries pentagon PQRST onto pentagon P′Q′R′S′T′. Which pair must be congruent?
S12-F2-Q4.grading_note: Each part corresponds to its own image.

S12-F2-Q5.skill: Use an established congruence to find unknown parts
S12-F2-Q5.prompt: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA by a rigid motion with A → C, B → D, C → A. m∠BAC = 3y° and m∠DCA = 42°. Find y.
S12-F2-Q5.grading_note: Any equivalent form. ∠BAC corresponds to ∠DCA, so 3y = 42.

S13-M-Q1.skill: Congruent triangles: a rigid motion exactly when all corresponding parts are congruent
S13-M-Q1.prompt: A rigid motion carries △ABC onto △DEF with A → D, B → E, C → F. Explain why AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = FD, ∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E, and ∠C ≅ ∠F.
S13-M-Q1.correct_answer: Each side and angle of ABC is carried onto the corresponding side and angle of DEF, and rigid motions keep lengths and angle measures.
S13-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) the motion maps segment AB onto segment DE (endpoints to endpoints), and similarly for the other sides and angles; (2) rigid motions preserve distance and angle measure. Invalid: "they look the same".
S13-M-Q1.required_method: Use the definition: the motion sends each vertex to its partner, so it sends each side and angle onto the corresponding one, and rigid motions keep length and angle measure.

S13-M-Q2.skill: Congruent triangles: a rigid motion exactly when all corresponding parts are congruent
S13-M-Q2.prompt: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = FD, ∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E, and ∠C ≅ ∠F. Explain how to build a rigid motion that carries △ABC onto △DEF.
S13-M-Q2.correct_answer: A translation, a rotation, and (if needed) a reflection carry A to D, B to E, and C to F.
S13-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the translation and rotation match A and B; the reflection (if needed) puts C on F's side; C lands on F because ∠A ≅ ∠D puts C on ray DF and AC = DF fixes its distance from D. Accept using ∠B and ∠E instead. Invalid: stating the result without explaining why C lands on F.
S13-M-Q2.required_method: Translate A to D; rotate about D so ray AB lies on ray DE (B lands on E because AB = DE); if C is on the other side of line DE from F, reflect across DE. Explain why C then lands on F.

S13-M-Q3.skill: Congruent triangles: a rigid motion exactly when all corresponding parts are congruent
S13-M-Q3.prompt: A rigid motion maps △PQR onto △XYZ with P → X, Q → Y, R → Z. Which must be true?
S13-M-Q3.grading_note: Side QR corresponds to side YZ.

S13-M-Q4.skill: Congruent triangles: a rigid motion exactly when all corresponding parts are congruent
S13-M-Q4.prompt: △JKL ≅ △MNO with J ↔ M, K ↔ N, L ↔ O. JK = 8, KL = 11, and m∠L = 37°. Find MN, NO, and m∠O.
S13-M-Q4.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.

S13-M-Q5.skill: Congruent triangles: a rigid motion exactly when all corresponding parts are congruent
S13-M-Q5.prompt: Two triangles whose three pairs of corresponding angles are congruent must be congruent.
S13-M-Q5.grading_note: A small and a large equilateral triangle have the same angles but are not congruent: the sides must match too.

S13-B1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The order of the letters gives the correspondence.

S13-B3-Q2.prompt: A ray starts at the origin and points along the positive x-axis. Which rotation about the origin makes it point along the positive y-axis?

S13-B3-Q3.skill: Move a point onto another and a ray onto another with rigid motions
S13-B3-Q3.prompt: After a rotation, point C is below line DE but should be above it, and D and E are on the line. Which motion moves C across without moving D or E?
choices: A rotation about the midpoint of DE
S13-B3-Q3.grading_note: A reflection across DE keeps every point of the line fixed.

S13-B3-Q4.skill: Move a point onto another and a ray onto another with rigid motions
S13-B3-Q4.prompt: Reflecting across a line keeps every point of that line fixed.
S13-B3-Q4.grading_note: Points on the mirror line are their own images.

S13-B3-Q5.skill: Move a point onto another and a ray onto another with rigid motions
S13-B3-Q5.prompt: Translating a triangle can keep exactly one of its vertices fixed.
S13-B3-Q5.grading_note: A nonzero translation moves every point.

S13-F1-Q1.skill: Find which three corresponding parts are enough
S13-F1-Q1.prompt: Must two triangles be congruent if all three pairs of corresponding sides are congruent? Use the result of the full six-part test.
S13-F1-Q1.correct_answer: Yes. Three congruent sides force the angles to be congruent too (SSS), so all six parts match and a rigid motion exists.

S13-F1-Q2.skill: Find which three corresponding parts are enough
S13-F1-Q2.prompt: Give an example of two triangles with two pairs of congruent sides and a pair of congruent angles that are NOT congruent.
S13-F1-Q2.correct_answer: Triangles with sides 6 and 8 and a 30° angle opposite the 6-unit side: the 8-unit side can make the third side either long or short (SSA).
S13-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any valid SSA counterexample with the angle not between the sides.

S13-F1-Q3.skill: Find which three corresponding parts are enough
S13-F1-Q3.prompt: Knowing that all three pairs of corresponding angles are congruent is enough to prove two triangles congruent.
S13-F1-Q3.grading_note: AAA gives similar triangles, not necessarily congruent ones.

S13-F1-Q4.skill: Find which three corresponding parts are enough
S13-F1-Q4.prompt: Which set of corresponding parts is NOT always enough for congruence?
choices: Two sides and an angle not between them
Two sides and the angle between them
Two angles and the side between them
S13-F1-Q4.correct_answer: Two sides and an angle not between them
S13-F1-Q4.grading_note: SSA can give two different triangles.

S13-F1-Q5.skill: Find which three corresponding parts are enough
S13-F1-Q5.prompt: Two triangles have AB = DE, ∠A ≅ ∠D, and ∠B ≅ ∠E. Must ∠C ≅ ∠F? Explain.
S13-F1-Q5.correct_answer: Yes. The angle sum is 180° in both triangles, so ∠C = 180° - ∠A - ∠B = ∠F.

S13-F2-Q1.skill: Use congruent triangles to prove a relationship in a figure
S13-F2-Q1.prompt: In quadrilateral ABCD, AB = CB and AD = CD. Prove that diagonal BD bisects ∠ABC.
S13-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: AB = CB, AD = CD, BD = BD (reflexive); SSS gives the congruence; corresponding angles ∠ABD and ∠CBD are congruent, which is the definition of a bisector. Invalid: assuming the angles are equal from the picture.
S13-F2-Q1.required_method: Prove △ABD ≅ △CBD (SSS, with BD shared), then use corresponding angles.

S13-F2-Q2.skill: Use congruent triangles to prove a relationship in a figure
S13-F2-Q2.prompt: Segments AC and BD bisect each other at E. Prove that AB = CD.
S13-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: AE = CE and BE = DE (definition of bisect); ∠AEB ≅ ∠CED (vertical angles); SAS; corresponding sides AB = CD.
S13-F2-Q2.required_method: Use vertical angles and the bisected segments to prove △AEB ≅ △CED by SAS.

S13-F2-Q3.skill: Use congruent triangles to prove a relationship in a figure
S13-F2-Q3.prompt: In △PQR and △STU, PQ = ST, QR = TU, and PR = SU. The triangles are congruent. What must be true of ∠R and ∠U? Why?
S13-F2-Q3.correct_answer: ∠R ≅ ∠U, because corresponding angles of congruent triangles are congruent.

S13-F2-Q4.skill: Use congruent triangles to prove a relationship in a figure
S13-F2-Q4.prompt: Once two triangles are proved congruent, only the parts used in the proof are known to be congruent.
S13-F2-Q4.grading_note: Congruence gives all six pairs of corresponding parts (CPCTC).

S13-F2-Q5.skill: Use congruent triangles to prove a relationship in a figure
S13-F2-Q5.prompt: To prove that point M is the midpoint of segment XY using congruent triangles, which pair of parts must you show is congruent?

S14-M-Q1.skill: Explain SAS congruence with rigid motions
S14-M-Q1.prompt: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE, AC = DF, and ∠A ≅ ∠D. Explain, using rigid motions, why △ABC ≅ △DEF.
S14-M-Q1.correct_answer: A translation, a rotation, and possibly a reflection carry A to D, B to E, and C to F, so the triangles are congruent.
S14-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) translate A onto D; (2) rotate about D so ray AB lies on ray DE; B lands on E because AB = DE; (3) reflect across DE if needed so C is on F's side; (4) ray AC lands on ray DF because ∠A ≅ ∠D; (5) C lands on F because AC = DF. Invalid: "the triangles look the same"; citing SAS to prove SAS.

figure.desc: Triangles ABC and DEF. AB and DE have one tick mark each, AC and DF have two tick marks each, and angles A and D have one arc each, showing AB = DE, AC = DF, and angle A congruent to angle D.

S14-M-Q1.required_method: Translate A to D; rotate so ray AB lies on ray DE; reflect across DE if C is on the other side from F. Then explain why B lands on E and C lands on F.

S14-M-Q2.skill: Explain SAS congruence with rigid motions
S14-M-Q2.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of SAS, A has been moved to D and ray AB lies on ray DE, with C on the same side of line DE as F. Why must ray AC lie on ray DF?
choices: ∠A ≅ ∠D, so both rays make the same angle with ray DE on the same side
S14-M-Q2.correct_answer: ∠A ≅ ∠D, so both rays make the same angle with ray DE on the same side
S14-M-Q2.grading_note: There is only one ray from D on that side of line DE making that angle with ray DE.

S14-M-Q3.skill: Explain SAS congruence with rigid motions
S14-M-Q3.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of SAS, ray AC now lies on ray DF. Why does C land exactly on F?
S14-M-Q3.correct_answer: AC = DF and rigid motions keep length, so C is the point of ray DF at distance DF from D, which is F.

S14-M-Q4.skill: Explain SAS congruence with rigid motions
S14-M-Q4.prompt: Explain why a reflection is sometimes needed in the rigid-motion proof of SAS, and why it does not move D or E.
S14-M-Q4.correct_answer: After the rotation, C may be on the opposite side of line DE from F. Reflecting across line DE moves it to F's side; D and E are on the line, so they stay fixed.
S14-M-Q4.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation with both parts.

S14-M-Q5.skill: Explain SAS congruence with rigid motions
S14-M-Q5.prompt: The rigid-motion argument for SAS still works if the congruent angle is not between the two congruent sides.
S14-M-Q5.grading_note: Then the angle does not fix where the third vertex goes; SSA can give two different triangles.

S14-B1-Q1.skill: Identify the included angle and included side
S14-B1-Q1.prompt: In △ABC, which angle is included between sides AB and AC?
S14-B1-Q1.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The included angle is at the shared vertex.

S14-B1-Q2.skill: Identify the included angle and included side
S14-B1-Q2.prompt: In △PQR, which side is included between ∠P and ∠Q?

S14-B1-Q3.skill: Identify the included angle and included side
S14-B1-Q3.prompt: In △XYZ, which angle is NOT included between sides XY and YZ?
choices: None of the angles is excluded
S14-B1-Q3.grading_note: Sides XY and YZ share vertex Y, so ∠Y is included; ∠X is not.

S14-B1-Q4.skill: Identify the included angle and included side
S14-B1-Q4.prompt: Two sides of 5 cm and 7 cm with a 40° angle between them determine one triangle.
S14-B1-Q4.grading_note: Two sides and the included angle fix the triangle.

S14-B1-Q5.skill: Identify the included angle and included side
S14-B1-Q5.prompt: Two sides of 5 cm and 7 cm with a 40° angle that is not between them always determine one triangle.
S14-B1-Q5.grading_note: When the angle is not between the sides, there may be two triangles or none.

S14-B2-Q1.prompt: Under a rigid motion, the image of a ray is a ray.

S14-B2-Q2.skill: Rigid motions map rays, lengths, and angles to equal ones

S14-B2-Q3.skill: Rigid motions map rays, lengths, and angles to equal ones
S14-B2-Q3.prompt: A point is 5 units from D along a ray. After a rotation about D, the image point is
choices: 5 units from D on the image ray
S14-B2-Q3.correct_answer: 5 units from D on the image ray
S14-B2-Q3.grading_note: A rotation about D keeps distances from D.

S14-B2-Q4.skill: Rigid motions map rays, lengths, and angles to equal ones
S14-B2-Q4.prompt: A reflection across line DE can move point D.
S14-B2-Q4.grading_note: Points on the mirror line stay fixed.

S14-B2-Q5.skill: Rigid motions map rays, lengths, and angles to equal ones
S14-B2-Q5.prompt: Segment AB is translated so that A lands on D. AB = 9. How far is the image of B from D?

S14-B3-Q1.skill: Choose a translation, rotation, or reflection to move a point or ray onto a target
S14-B3-Q1.prompt: Which kind of rigid motion moves point A onto point D without turning anything?

S14-B3-Q2.skill: Choose a translation, rotation, or reflection to move a point or ray onto a target
S14-B3-Q2.prompt: A and D are already together. Which kind of rigid motion turns ray AB onto ray DE without moving D?

S14-B3-Q3.skill: Choose a translation, rotation, or reflection to move a point or ray onto a target
S14-B3-Q3.prompt: D and E are fixed, and point C is on the wrong side of line DE. Which motion fixes D and E and moves C across the line?
S14-B3-Q3.grading_note: Only the reflection keeps both D and E fixed.

S14-B3-Q4.skill: Choose a translation, rotation, or reflection to move a point or ray onto a target
S14-B3-Q4.prompt: A rotation about point D keeps D fixed.
S14-B3-Q4.grading_note: The center of a rotation is its own image.

S14-B3-Q5.skill: Choose a translation, rotation, or reflection to move a point or ray onto a target
S14-B3-Q5.prompt: A translation that moves A onto D also keeps A fixed.

S14-F1-Q1.skill: Prove triangles congruent by SAS inside a larger figure
S14-F1-Q1.prompt: In quadrilateral ABCD, AB ∥ DC and AB = DC. Diagonal AC is drawn. Prove that △ABC ≅ △CDA.
S14-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: AB = CD (given); ∠BAC ≅ ∠DCA (alternate interior angles, AB ∥ DC); AC = CA (reflexive); SAS with the angle between the sides. Invalid: using ∠B ≅ ∠D without proof.
S14-F1-Q1.required_method: Use alternate interior angles with the parallel sides and the shared diagonal to apply SAS.

S14-F1-Q2.skill: Prove triangles congruent by SAS inside a larger figure
S14-F1-Q2.prompt: Point M is the midpoint of segment AB, and line ℓ is perpendicular to AB at M. Point P is on ℓ. Prove that △PMA ≅ △PMB.
S14-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: AM = BM (midpoint); ∠PMA ≅ ∠PMB (both right angles); PM = PM; SAS.
S14-F1-Q2.required_method: Use the midpoint, the right angles, and the shared side PM with SAS.

S14-F1-Q3.skill: Prove triangles congruent by SAS inside a larger figure
S14-F1-Q3.prompt: Segments AC and BD cross at E, with AE = CE and BE = DE. Name the congruent triangles and the criterion.
S14-F1-Q3.correct_answer: △AEB ≅ △CED by SAS (the vertical angles at E are the included angles).

S14-F1-Q4.skill: Prove triangles congruent by SAS inside a larger figure
S14-F1-Q4.prompt: In an SAS proof, a side that the two triangles share can be one of the pairs of congruent sides.
S14-F1-Q4.grading_note: The shared side is congruent to itself (reflexive property).

S14-F1-Q5.skill: Prove triangles congruent by SAS inside a larger figure
S14-F1-Q5.prompt: Segments PQ and RS bisect each other at T. Which reason gives the included angles for SAS?
choices: The angles are both right angles
S14-F1-Q5.grading_note: ∠PTR and ∠QTS (or the other pair) are vertical angles.

S14-F2-Q1.skill: Decide whether given information is enough for SAS, and name a missing condition
S14-F2-Q1.prompt: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE and BC = EF. Name ONE more pair of congruent parts that would prove congruence by SAS.
S14-F2-Q1.grading_note: Form required: the included angle pair. (AC = DF would give SSS, not SAS.)

S14-F2-Q2.skill: Decide whether given information is enough for SAS, and name a missing condition
S14-F2-Q2.prompt: In △PQR and △XYZ, PQ = XY, PR = XZ, and ∠Q ≅ ∠Y. Is this enough to prove the triangles congruent? Explain.
S14-F2-Q2.correct_answer: No. The congruent angle is not between the congruent sides (SSA), which does not guarantee congruence.

S14-F2-Q3.skill: Decide whether given information is enough for SAS, and name a missing condition
S14-F2-Q3.prompt: In △ABC and △ADC (sharing AC), AB = AD and ∠BCA ≅ ∠DCA. These facts prove △ABC ≅ △ADC by SAS.
S14-F2-Q3.grading_note: The congruent angles at C are not included between AB and AC (this is SSA), so SAS does not apply.

S14-F2-Q4.skill: Decide whether given information is enough for SAS, and name a missing condition
S14-F2-Q4.prompt: Kites ABCD and EFGH have AB = EF, BC = FG, and ∠B ≅ ∠F. Which triangles are congruent by SAS?
S14-F2-Q4.grading_note: The given parts are the two sides and the included angle of △ABC and △EFG.

S14-F2-Q5.skill: Decide whether given information is enough for SAS, and name a missing condition
S14-F2-Q5.prompt: Two triangles have sides 7 and 9 with a 50° angle between them. A student says they need not be congruent because the third sides were not measured. Is the student right? Explain.
S14-F2-Q5.correct_answer: No. SAS guarantees congruence; the third side is then determined (and equal).

S15-M-Q1.skill: Explain ASA congruence with rigid motions
S15-M-Q1.prompt: In △ABC and △DEF, ∠A ≅ ∠D, AB = DE, and ∠B ≅ ∠E. Explain, using rigid motions, why △ABC ≅ △DEF.
S15-M-Q1.correct_answer: A translation, a rotation, and possibly a reflection carry A to D, B to E, and C to F.
S15-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) A → D and B → E using AB = DE; (2) C on F's side of DE (reflect if needed); (3) ray AC lands on ray DF because ∠A ≅ ∠D; (4) ray BC lands on ray EF because ∠B ≅ ∠E; (5) C is where rays AC and BC meet, so it lands where DF and EF meet, which is F. Invalid: using side lengths AC or BC (not given); citing ASA to prove ASA.

figure.desc: Triangles ABC and DEF. AB and DE have one tick mark each; angles A and D have one arc each; angles B and E have two arcs each. So AB = DE, angle A is congruent to angle D, and angle B is congruent to angle E.

S15-M-Q1.required_method: Translate A to D; rotate so ray AB lies on ray DE (B lands on E); reflect across DE if needed; then use the two angles to place rays AC and BC on rays DF and EF.

S15-M-Q2.skill: Explain ASA congruence with rigid motions
S15-M-Q2.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of ASA, A is on D, B is on E, and C is on F's side of line DE. Why does C land on F?
choices: C and F are both the highest points
C is where rays AC and BC meet; those rays now lie on rays DF and EF, which meet only at F
S15-M-Q2.correct_answer: C is where rays AC and BC meet; those rays now lie on rays DF and EF, which meet only at F
S15-M-Q2.grading_note: The two angles place the two rays; the intersection point is unique.

S15-M-Q3.skill: Explain ASA congruence with rigid motions
S15-M-Q3.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of ASA, A is on D, B is on E, and C is on the same side of line DE as F. Explain why ray BC lies on ray EF.
S15-M-Q3.correct_answer: ∠B ≅ ∠E, and on that side of line DE there is only one ray from E making that angle with ray ED, namely ray EF.

S15-M-Q4.skill: Explain ASA congruence with rigid motions
S15-M-Q4.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of ASA, why can rays DF and EF meet in only one point?
S15-M-Q4.correct_answer: They lie on two different lines, and two different lines meet in at most one point.

S15-M-Q5.skill: Explain ASA congruence with rigid motions
S15-M-Q5.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of ASA, a reflection across line DE leaves D and E where they are.
S15-M-Q5.grading_note: Points on the line of reflection are fixed.

S15-B1-Q1.skill: Two angles and the included side determine a triangle
S15-B1-Q1.prompt: Two angles of 40° and 60° with a 5 cm side between them determine exactly one triangle (up to position).

S15-B1-Q2.skill: Two angles and the included side determine a triangle

S15-B1-Q3.skill: Two angles and the included side determine a triangle

One angle of 45° and nothing else

S15-B1-Q4.correct_answer: Angles 30° and 80° with a 4 cm side between them

S15-B1-Q5.skill: Two angles and the included side determine a triangle
S15-B1-Q5.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are 95° and 90°. Can the triangle exist? Explain.

S15-B3-Q4.skill: Rigid motions keep rays and angle measures

S15-F1-Q1.skill: Explain AAS from ASA and the triangle angle sum
S15-F1-Q1.prompt: In △ABC and △DEF, ∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E, and BC = EF (the side is NOT between the angles). Prove △ABC ≅ △DEF.
S15-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: m∠C = 180° - m∠A - m∠B = 180° - m∠D - m∠E = m∠F; then ∠B, side BC, ∠C match ∠E, EF, ∠F (ASA).
S15-F1-Q1.required_method: Use the triangle angle sum to show ∠C ≅ ∠F, then apply ASA with ∠B, BC, ∠C.

S15-F1-Q2.skill: Explain AAS from ASA and the triangle angle sum
S15-F1-Q2.prompt: Two triangles have angles 40° and 75° and a 9 cm side opposite the 75° angle. Must they be congruent? Explain.
S15-F1-Q2.correct_answer: Yes, by AAS: the third angles are both 65°, so ASA applies.

S15-F1-Q3.skill: Explain AAS from ASA and the triangle angle sum
S15-F1-Q3.prompt: AAS is a valid congruence criterion only because the angles of a triangle add to 180°.
S15-F1-Q3.grading_note: The angle sum gives the third pair of angles, turning AAS into ASA.

S15-F1-Q4.skill: Explain AAS from ASA and the triangle angle sum
S15-F1-Q4.prompt: In △PQR and △XYZ, ∠P ≅ ∠X, ∠Q ≅ ∠Y, and PR = XZ. Which criterion proves congruence?
S15-F1-Q4.grading_note: PR is not between ∠P and ∠Q, so it is AAS.

S15-F1-Q5.skill: Explain AAS from ASA and the triangle angle sum
S15-F1-Q5.prompt: Which corresponding side would make AAS apply if ∠A ≅ ∠D and ∠C ≅ ∠F?
S15-F1-Q5.grading_note: Any side not between the two angles (AC = DF would be ASA).

S15-F2-Q1.skill: Prove congruence with ASA or AAS in overlapping triangles
S15-F2-Q1.prompt: Segments AD and BC cross at E. AB ∥ CD and E is the midpoint of AD. Prove that △ABE ≅ △DCE.
S15-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: ∠BAE ≅ ∠CDE (alternate interior, AB ∥ CD); AE = DE (midpoint); ∠AEB ≅ ∠DEC (vertical); ASA. AAS with ∠B ≅ ∠C also accepted.
S15-F2-Q1.required_method: Use alternate interior angles, the vertical angles at E, and AE = DE with ASA.

S15-F2-Q2.skill: Prove congruence with ASA or AAS in overlapping triangles
S15-F2-Q2.prompt: In △ABC, the bisector of ∠A is perpendicular to BC at D. Prove that AB = AC.
S15-F2-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: ∠BAD ≅ ∠CAD (bisector); AD = AD; ∠ADB ≅ ∠ADC (right angles); ASA; corresponding sides.
S15-F2-Q2.required_method: Prove △ABD ≅ △ACD by ASA using the bisected angle, the shared side AD, and the right angles.

S15-F2-Q3.skill: Prove congruence with ASA or AAS in overlapping triangles
S15-F2-Q3.prompt: In overlapping triangles ABE and ACD, ∠A is shared, AB = AC, and ∠B ≅ ∠C. Which criterion proves △ABE ≅ △ACD?
S15-F2-Q3.grading_note: Form required: the criterion with the matching parts.

S15-F2-Q4.skill: Prove congruence with ASA or AAS in overlapping triangles
S15-F2-Q4.prompt: An angle shared by two overlapping triangles cannot be used in a congruence proof, because it is the same angle.
S15-F2-Q4.grading_note: By the reflexive property, the shared angle is congruent to itself and can be used.

S15-F2-Q5.skill: Prove congruence with ASA or AAS in overlapping triangles
S15-F2-Q5.prompt: In △JKL and △JML, ∠KJL ≅ ∠MJL and ∠JLK ≅ ∠JLM. Which side completes ASA?
S15-F2-Q5.grading_note: JL is between the two pairs of angles and is shared.

S16-M-Q1.skill: Explain SSS congruence with rigid motions
S16-M-Q1.prompt: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE, BC = EF, and CA = FD. Explain, using rigid motions, why △ABC ≅ △DEF.
S16-M-Q1.correct_answer: A translation and a rotation carry A to D and B to E; if needed, the reflection across DE carries C′ to F.
S16-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) A → D, B → E (AB = DE); (2) DC′ = DF and EC′ = EF (rigid motions keep lengths); (3) if C′ ≠ F, D and E are each equidistant from C′ and F, so line DE is the perpendicular bisector of C′F; (4) the reflection across DE fixes D and E and maps C′ to F. Alternative: C′ and F both lie on the circles centered at D and E with these radii, which meet in at most one point on each side of DE. Invalid: using angles (none are given); citing SSS to prove SSS.

figure.desc: Triangles ABC and DEF with matching tick marks: AB and DE one tick, AC and DF two ticks, BC and EF three ticks, so all three pairs of sides are congruent.

S16-M-Q1.required_method: Move A to D and B to E (translation and rotation, using AB = DE). If the image C′ of C is not F, show that line DE is the perpendicular bisector of C′F, so the reflection across DE carries C′ to F.

S16-M-Q2.skill: Explain SSS congruence with rigid motions
S16-M-Q2.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of SSS, A is on D, B is on E, and C′ (the image of C) is not F. Why is line DE the perpendicular bisector of C′F?
choices: D and E are each the same distance from C′ as from F
S16-M-Q2.correct_answer: D and E are each the same distance from C′ as from F
S16-M-Q2.grading_note: A point equidistant from C′ and F lies on the perpendicular bisector of C′F; two such points determine that line.

S16-M-Q3.skill: Explain SSS congruence with rigid motions
S16-M-Q3.prompt: In the rigid-motion proof of SSS, line DE is the perpendicular bisector of C′F. Why does the reflection across DE carry C′ onto F, and why is that enough?
S16-M-Q3.correct_answer: By the definition of a reflection, it maps C′ to F because DE is the perpendicular bisector of C′F; it keeps D and E fixed, so the whole triangle lands on DEF.
S16-M-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation with both parts.

S16-M-Q4.skill: Explain SSS congruence with rigid motions
S16-M-Q4.prompt: The rigid-motion proof of SSS uses no angle information. Explain how the three side lengths alone locate the third vertex.
S16-M-Q4.correct_answer: Once D and E are matched, the third vertex must be DF from D and EF from E: it lies on two circles, which meet in at most one point on each side of DE.

S16-M-Q5.skill: Explain SSS congruence with rigid motions
S16-M-Q5.prompt: A triangle with sides 5, 7, and 9 is congruent to a triangle with sides 9, 5, and 7.
S16-M-Q5.grading_note: Matching the sides by length gives three pairs of congruent sides (SSS).

S16-B1-Q3.skill: Three side lengths determine a triangle (triangle inequality)

S16-B1-Q4.skill: Three side lengths determine a triangle (triangle inequality)

S16-B2-Q2.prompt: All points 3 cm from a point A form a circle with center A and radius 3 cm.

S16-B2-Q3.skill: Find the points at given distances from two points (two circles)
S16-B2-Q3.prompt: Circles of radius 4 centered at A and B meet at two points. AB = 6. Where are the two points?

Both on the same side of AB

S16-B2-Q4.skill: Find the points at given distances from two points (two circles)

S16-B2-Q5.skill: Find the points at given distances from two points (two circles)

S16-B2-Q5.correct_answer: No. 3 + 4 = 7 < 10, so the circles do not meet.

S16-F1-Q1.skill: Explain the Hypotenuse-Leg criterion for right triangles
S16-F1-Q1.prompt: Right triangles ABC and DEF have right angles at C and F, hypotenuses AB = DE, and legs AC = DF. Prove that △ABC ≅ △DEF.
S16-F1-Q1.correct_answer: △ABC ≅ △DEF by SSS (BC = EF from the Pythagorean Theorem).
S16-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: BC = √(AB² - AC²) = √(DE² - DF²) = EF; then SSS.
S16-F1-Q1.required_method: Use the Pythagorean Theorem to show BC = EF, then apply SSS.

S16-F1-Q2.skill: Explain the Hypotenuse-Leg criterion for right triangles
S16-F1-Q2.prompt: Two right triangles each have hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. Are they congruent? What is the other leg?
S16-F1-Q2.correct_answer: Yes; the other leg is 12 in both.

S16-F1-Q3.skill: Explain the Hypotenuse-Leg criterion for right triangles
S16-F1-Q3.prompt: Hypotenuse-Leg is a special case of SSA that does guarantee congruence.

S16-F2-Q1.correct_answer: Equilateral triangles with sides 2 and 5 have all angles 60° but are not congruent.

S16-F2-Q2.skill: Decide which criteria guarantee congruence, with counterexamples

S16-F2-Q3.skill: Decide which criteria guarantee congruence, with counterexamples

S16-F2-Q4.skill: Decide which criteria guarantee congruence, with counterexamples
S16-F2-Q4.prompt: If two triangles have the same three side lengths, they have the same three angle measures.
S16-F2-Q4.grading_note: SSS gives congruence, and corresponding angles of congruent triangles are congruent.

S16-F2-Q5.skill: Decide which criteria guarantee congruence, with counterexamples
S16-F2-Q5.prompt: Two triangles with two pairs of congruent sides and equal areas must be congruent.
S16-F2-Q5.grading_note: The included angles could be θ and 180° - θ: equal areas (same sine), different third sides.

S17-M-Q1.skill: Prove that vertical angles are congruent
S17-M-Q1.prompt: Lines AB and CD intersect at E. Prove that ∠AEC ≅ ∠BED.
S17-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: (1) m∠AEC + m∠CEB = 180° (linear pair: A, E, B are collinear); (2) m∠CEB + m∠BED = 180° (linear pair: C, E, D are collinear); (3) so m∠AEC + m∠CEB = m∠CEB + m∠BED (substitution/transitive); (4) subtract m∠CEB. Alternative: the 180° rotation about E maps ray EA to ray EB and ray EC to ray ED. Invalid: "they look equal", measuring, or citing the theorem itself.

figure.desc: Lines AB and CD cross at point E. A and B are on one line, C and D on the other, with E between A and B and between C and D.

S17-M-Q1.required_method: Use the two linear pairs that share ∠CEB, and the subtraction property of equality.

S17-M-Q2.skill: Prove that vertical angles are congruent
S17-M-Q2.prompt: Lines ℓ and m meet at O, forming ∠1, ∠2, ∠3, and ∠4 in order around O. Prove that ∠2 ≅ ∠4.
S17-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: m∠1 + m∠2 = 180° and m∠1 + m∠4 = 180° (linear pairs, each with a reason); so m∠2 = 180° - m∠1 = m∠4. Using ∠3 as the shared angle is also valid. Invalid: using ∠2 ≅ ∠4 as a step.

figure.desc: Lines ℓ and m cross at point O, forming four angles numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 in counterclockwise order. Angles 1 and 3 are vertical angles, and so are angles 2 and 4.

S17-M-Q2.required_method: Use the linear pairs ∠1 and ∠2, and ∠1 and ∠4, then the subtraction property of equality.

S17-M-Q3.skill: Prove that vertical angles are congruent
S17-M-Q3.prompt:
A proof that ∠1 ≅ ∠3 for vertical angles 1 and 3 (with ∠2 next to both):
1. m∠1 + m∠2 = 180°  (linear pair)
2. m∠2 + m∠3 = 180°  (linear pair)
3. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠2 + m∠3  (?)
4. m∠1 = m∠3  (?)
Give the reasons for steps 3 and 4.
S17-M-Q3.correct_answer: Step 3: substitution (or the transitive property of equality); step 4: subtraction property of equality.
S17-M-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent names for both reasons. Both are required.

S17-M-Q4.skill: Prove that vertical angles are congruent
S17-M-Q4.prompt: Lines AB and CD intersect at E. Explain, using a rigid motion, why ∠AEC ≅ ∠BED.
S17-M-Q4.correct_answer: The 180° rotation about E maps ∠AEC onto ∠BED, so the angles are congruent.
S17-M-Q4.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: a 180° rotation about E maps each line through E onto itself, sending ray EA to the opposite ray EB and ray EC to ray ED; so it maps ∠AEC onto ∠BED; rotations keep angle measures.

figure.desc: Lines AB and CD cross at point E. A and B are on one line, C and D on the other, with E between A and B and between C and D.

S17-M-Q4.required_method: Use the 180° rotation about E and explain where it sends rays EA and EC.

S17-M-Q5.skill: Prove that vertical angles are congruent
S17-M-Q5.prompt: A student measures two vertical angles in one drawing, finds that both are 47°, and writes "vertical angles are congruent." Why is this not a proof?
choices: Vertical angles are not always congruent
It checks one example; a proof must show the result for every pair of vertical angles
The student should have measured all four angles
S17-M-Q5.correct_answer: It checks one example; a proof must show the result for every pair of vertical angles
S17-M-Q5.grading_note: Measuring can suggest a theorem but cannot prove it for all cases.

S17-B1-Q4.skill: Angles in a linear pair add to 180°

S17-F1-Q1.skill: Use the vertical angle theorem in multistep proofs
S17-F1-Q1.prompt: Lines AB and CD intersect at E, and ray EF bisects ∠AEC. Ray EG is the ray opposite ray EF. Prove that ray EG bisects ∠BED.
S17-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: m∠AEF = m∠FEC (bisector); ∠AEF ≅ ∠BEG and ∠FEC ≅ ∠DEG (vertical angles, since EG is opposite EF, EB opposite EA, ED opposite EC); so m∠BEG = m∠GED.
S17-F1-Q1.required_method: Combine the bisector definition with vertical angles (∠AEF and ∠BEG; ∠FEC and ∠GED).

S17-F1-Q2.skill: Use the vertical angle theorem in multistep proofs
S17-F1-Q2.prompt: Three lines meet at point O, forming six angles. Two of the angles that are next to each other are 50° and 70°. Prove that the six angles are 50°, 70°, 60°, 50°, 70°, 60° in order.
S17-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: three adjacent angles on one side of a line add to 180°, so the third is 60°; each of the other three is vertical to one of these.
S17-F1-Q2.required_method: Use the straight angle (180°) to find the third angle on one side, then vertical angles for the other three.

S17-F1-Q3.skill: Use the vertical angle theorem in multistep proofs
S17-F1-Q3.prompt: Two lines meet. One angle is (4x + 10)° and its vertical angle is (6x - 30)°. Find x and all four angles.
S17-F1-Q3.grading_note: Form required: x and the four angles. 4x + 10 = 6x - 30 gives x = 20, so the angle is 90°.

S17-F1-Q4.skill: Use the vertical angle theorem in multistep proofs
S17-F1-Q4.prompt: If one angle formed by two crossing lines is a right angle, all four angles are right angles.
S17-F1-Q4.grading_note: Its vertical angle is 90° and its neighbors are 180° - 90°.

S17-F1-Q5.skill: Use the vertical angle theorem in multistep proofs
S17-F1-Q5.prompt: Lines AB and CD meet at E with m∠AEC = 2x and m∠CEB = 3x. What is m∠BED?
S17-F1-Q5.grading_note: 2x + 3x = 180, so x = 36 and m∠AEC = 72°; ∠BED is vertical to ∠AEC.

S17-F2-Q1.skill: Prove statements about the bisectors of angles formed by two lines
S17-F2-Q1.prompt: ∠ABD and ∠DBC form a linear pair. Ray BE bisects ∠ABD and ray BF bisects ∠DBC. Prove that ∠EBF is a right angle.
S17-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: m∠EBD = ½m∠ABD, m∠DBF = ½m∠DBC (bisectors); m∠EBF = ½(m∠ABD + m∠DBC) = ½(180°) = 90°.
S17-F2-Q1.required_method: Express m∠EBF as half of m∠ABD plus half of m∠DBC.

S17-F2-Q2.skill: Prove statements about the bisectors of angles formed by two lines
S17-F2-Q2.prompt: Is the converse of the vertical angle theorem true: "If two angles are congruent, they are vertical angles"? Explain.

S17-F2-Q3.skill: Prove statements about the bisectors of angles formed by two lines
S17-F2-Q3.prompt: Two lines meet at O. Prove that the bisectors of a pair of vertical angles lie on one line.
S17-F2-Q3.correct_answer: The bisector rays are opposite rays, so they lie on one line.
S17-F2-Q3.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: if the vertical angles each measure 2a and the other two each 180° - 2a, the angle from one bisector to the other is a + (180° - 2a) + a = 180°.
S17-F2-Q3.required_method: Show that the angle between the two bisector rays is 180°.

S17-F2-Q4.skill: Prove statements about the bisectors of angles formed by two lines
S17-F2-Q4.prompt: The bisectors of a pair of vertical angles are perpendicular.
S17-F2-Q4.grading_note: They form one straight line: each bisector is the extension of the other.

S17-F2-Q5.skill: Prove statements about the bisectors of angles formed by two lines

S17-F2-Q5.grading_note: Adjacent angles formed by two lines are a linear pair, so their bisectors meet at 90°.

S18-M-Q3.skill: Prove the angle theorems for parallel lines cut by a transversal

S18-F1-Q1.skill: Prove the converse: congruent alternate interior angles make lines parallel
S18-F1-Q1.prompt: Lines ℓ and m are cut by transversal t, and alternate interior angles ∠3 and ∠5 are congruent. Prove that ℓ ∥ m.
S18-F1-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential (indirect): if ℓ and m met at a point R, triangle PQR would have an exterior angle equal to a remote interior angle, which is impossible (an exterior angle is greater than each remote interior angle); so they do not meet. Alternative: the 180° rotation about the midpoint of PQ swaps P and Q and maps ℓ onto m, so if they met on one side they would also meet on the other, giving two common points. Invalid: assuming ℓ ∥ m.

S18-F1-Q1.required_method: Indirect proof: suppose ℓ and m meet; they would form a triangle with t whose angles contradict a known result. Or use the 180° rotation about the midpoint of PQ.

S18-F1-Q2.skill: Prove the converse: congruent alternate interior angles make lines parallel
S18-F1-Q2.prompt: Lines ℓ and m are cut by transversal t with m∠4 = (5x - 20)° and m∠6 = (3x + 30)°. For what value of x is ℓ ∥ m? Explain.
S18-F1-Q2.correct_answer: x = 25, because then the alternate interior angles are congruent (105°).
S18-F1-Q2.grading_note: Form required: x with the converse as the reason. 5x - 20 = 3x + 30.

S18-F1-Q4.skill: Prove the converse: congruent alternate interior angles make lines parallel
S18-F1-Q4.prompt: Which fact proves that lines ℓ and m are parallel?
choices: A pair of corresponding angles is congruent
A pair of vertical angles is congruent
Two angles at the same crossing are equal

S18-F1-Q5.skill: Prove the converse: congruent alternate interior angles make lines parallel
S18-F1-Q5.prompt: Lines ℓ and m are cut by a transversal. m∠1 = 72° and m∠7 = 108°. Are ℓ and m parallel? Explain.

S18-F1-Q5.grading_note: Form required: the conclusion with a reason. Equivalently, ∠5 is vertical to ∠7, so m∠5 = 108°, but its corresponding angle ∠1 is 72°.

S18-F2-Q1.required_method: Name the two new angles at B, use alternate interior angles, and the straight angle at B.

S18-F2-Q2.skill: Use parallel-line theorems to prove the triangle angle sum
S18-F2-Q2.prompt: In triangle ABC, a line through B parallel to AC makes a 50° angle with BA (on A's side) and a 65° angle with BC (on C's side). Find all three angles of the triangle.
S18-F2-Q2.grading_note: Form required: all three. Alternate interior angles give ∠A and ∠C; 180 - 50 - 65 = 65.

S18-F2-Q3.skill: Use parallel-line theorems to prove the triangle angle sum
S18-F2-Q3.prompt: The proof of the triangle angle sum works without any fact about parallel lines.
S18-F2-Q3.grading_note: It uses the parallel through one vertex and the alternate interior angle theorem.

S18-F2-Q4.skill: Use parallel-line theorems to prove the triangle angle sum
S18-F2-Q4.prompt: Which theorem is used to show the new angles at B equal ∠A and ∠C?
S18-F2-Q4.grading_note: Sides BA and BC are transversals of the parallel lines (AC and the line through B).

S18-F2-Q5.skill: Use parallel-line theorems to prove the triangle angle sum
S18-F2-Q5.prompt: Explain why the exterior angle at C of triangle ABC equals m∠A + m∠B.
S18-F2-Q5.correct_answer: The exterior angle forms a linear pair with ∠C, so it is 180° - m∠C, which equals m∠A + m∠B by the angle sum.

S19-M-Q1.skill: Prove the perpendicular bisector theorem and its converse
S19-M-Q1.prompt: Line ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of segment AB, meeting AB at M. Point P is on ℓ. Prove that PA = PB.
S19-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: AM = BM (M is the midpoint); ∠PMA ≅ ∠PMB (both right angles, ℓ ⊥ AB); PM = PM (reflexive); △PMA ≅ △PMB (SAS); PA = PB (corresponding parts). If P = M, PA = MA = MB = PB directly. Alternative: the reflection across ℓ fixes P and swaps A and B.

figure.desc: Segment AB with midpoint M (AM and MB marked congruent). Line ℓ is perpendicular to AB at M (right-angle mark). Point P is on ℓ above AB; dashed segments join P to A and to B.

S19-M-Q1.required_method: Use SAS on triangles PMA and PMB.

S19-M-Q2.skill: Prove the perpendicular bisector theorem and its converse
S19-M-Q2.prompt: Point P is not on line AB, and PA = PB. Let M be the midpoint of AB. Prove that line PM is perpendicular to AB, so P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
S19-M-Q2.correct_answer: PM ⊥ AB, so P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
S19-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: PA = PB (given), AM = BM (midpoint), PM = PM; △PMA ≅ △PMB (SSS); ∠PMA ≅ ∠PMB; they form a linear pair, so each is 90°; so PM is perpendicular to AB through its midpoint. Invalid: drawing the perpendicular bisector through P and assuming it passes through P (that is the claim).
S19-M-Q2.required_method: Use SSS on triangles PMA and PMB, then the linear pair of congruent angles at M.

S19-M-Q3.skill: Prove the perpendicular bisector theorem and its converse
S19-M-Q3.prompt: The theorem says the points on the perpendicular bisector of AB are EXACTLY the points equidistant from A and B. Which two statements must be proved?
S19-M-Q3.correct_answer: (1) Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from A and B. (2) Every point equidistant from A and B is on the perpendicular bisector.
S19-M-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent wording of both directions.

S19-M-Q4.skill: Prove the perpendicular bisector theorem and its converse
S19-M-Q4.prompt: In a coordinate plane, A(-a, 0) and B(a, 0) with a > 0. Prove that every point P(0, y) on the y-axis is equidistant from A and B, and that every point P(x, y) with PA = PB has x = 0.

S22-M-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC has A(0, 0), B(2a, 0), and C(2b, 2c), with a > 0 and c ≠ 0. D is the midpoint of AC and E is the midpoint of BC. Prove that DE ∥ AB and DE = ½AB.
S22-M-Q1.correct_answer: D(b, c), E(a + b, c); DE is horizontal like AB, and DE = a = ½(2a) = ½AB.
S22-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: both midpoints; DE has slope 0 (same y) and AB has slope 0, so DE ∥ AB (and DE ≠ AB since c ≠ 0); DE = |a + b - b| = a and AB = 2a. Invalid: checking one numerical triangle only.
S22-M-Q1.required_method: Find D and E with the midpoint formula, then compare slopes and lengths.

S22-M-Q2.prompt: In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of AC and E is the midpoint of BC. Extend DE past E to F so that EF = DE. Prove that DE ∥ AB and DE = ½AB.
S22-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: CE = BE, DE = FE, vertical angles at E, so △DEC ≅ △FEB (SAS); BF = DC = AD; ∠DCE ≅ ∠FBE gives BF ∥ AC (alternate interior converse); one pair of opposite sides of ABFD is parallel and congruent, so ABFD is a parallelogram; so DF ∥ AB and DF = AB; DE = ½DF = ½AB.

S22-M-Q3.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that mentions avoiding fractions in the midpoint formula and that the placement is general.

S22-M-Q4.prompt:
A proof of the midsegment theorem with A(0, 0), B(2a, 0), C(2b, 2c):

2. slope DE = 0 = slope AB  (?)
3. DE ∥ AB  (?)
4. DE = a and AB = 2a, so DE = ½AB  (?)
Give the four reasons.

S23-M-Q1.skill: Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at one point
S23-M-Q1.prompt: Triangle ABC has A(0, 0), B(2b, 0), and C(2c, 2d), with b ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0. Prove that the point G((2b + 2c)/3, 2d/3) lies on all three medians.
S23-M-Q1.correct_answer: G is on the median from A (to (b + c, d)), from B (to (c, d)), and from C (to (b, 0)), so the medians meet at G.
S23-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: the three midpoints (b + c, d), (c, d), (b, 0); for each median, G = vertex + ⅔(midpoint - vertex): A + ⅔((b + c, d) - A) = G; B + ⅔((c, d) - (2b, 0)) = G; C + ⅔((b, 0) - (2c, 2d)) = G. Alternative: show G satisfies each median's equation. Invalid: checking one triangle with numbers.
S23-M-Q1.required_method: Find the midpoint of each side, then show G is two-thirds of the way from each vertex to the opposite midpoint (or on each median line).

S23-M-Q2.skill: Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at one point
S23-M-Q2.prompt: In triangle ABC, medians BE and CF meet at G. Let H and K be the midpoints of BG and CG. Prove that BG = 2GE. Then explain why the third median also passes through G.
S23-M-Q2.correct_answer: BG = 2GE; the same argument for medians AD and BE gives the point that is two-thirds along BE, which is G, so AD passes through G.
S23-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: FE ∥ BC and FE = ½BC (midsegment in △ABC); HK ∥ BC and HK = ½BC (midsegment in △GBC); so FEKH is a parallelogram; its diagonals bisect each other, so HG = GE; with BH = HG, BG = 2GE; any two medians meet at the point two-thirds along each, so all three share it.
S23-M-Q2.required_method: Use the midsegment theorem in triangles ABC and GBC to show FEKH is a parallelogram, then its diagonals.

S23-M-Q3.skill: Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at one point

S23-M-Q3.correct_answer: Each median contains its own two-thirds point. If those three points are one point, that point lies on all three medians, so they meet there.

S23-M-Q4.skill: Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at one point

(This proves the claim for this triangle; the general proof needs variables.)
S23-M-Q4.required_method: Find each median as a line through a vertex and a midpoint, find where two meet, and check that the third passes through that point.

S24-F1-Q1.skill: Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular

Essential: BE = ED (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other); AB = AD; AE = AE; △AEB ≅ △AED (SSS); ∠AEB ≅ ∠AED form a linear pair, so both are 90°. Alternative: A and C are each equidistant from B and D, so AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD.
S24-F1-Q1.required_method: Use that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, then SSS on triangles AEB and AED (or the perpendicular bisector converse).

S24-F2-Q1.skill: Prove the parallelogram properties with coordinates
S24-F2-Q1.prompt: A parallelogram has vertices A(0, 0), B(a, 0), C(a + b, c), D(b, c), with a > 0 and c > 0. Prove that AB = DC and AD = BC.
S24-F2-Q1.correct_answer: AB = DC = a and AD = BC = √(b² + c²)
S24-F2-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: AB = a; DC = |a + b - b| = a; AD = √(b² + c²); BC = √((a + b - a)² + c²) = √(b² + c²).
S24-F2-Q1.required_method: Use the distance formula on each pair of opposite sides.

S24-F2-Q2.skill: Prove the parallelogram properties with coordinates
S24-F2-Q2.prompt: Explain why the vertices A(0, 0), B(a, 0), C(a + b, c), D(b, c) describe a general parallelogram.
S24-F2-Q2.correct_answer: Any parallelogram can be moved (rigid motion) so that A is at the origin and AB lies on the positive x-axis; then D = (b, c) and C = B + (D - A) = (a + b, c).

S24-F2-Q3.skill: Prove the parallelogram properties with coordinates
S24-F2-Q3.prompt: With vertices A(0, 0), B(a, 0), C(a + b, c), D(b, c), slopes show AC ⊥ BD for every choice of a, b, and c.
S24-F2-Q3.grading_note: The product of the slopes is c²/(b² - a²), which is -1 only when a² = b² + c² (a rhombus).

S24-F2-Q4.skill: Prove the parallelogram properties with coordinates

Essential: AB = CD (opposite sides of a parallelogram); ∠BAE ≅ ∠DCE and ∠ABE ≅ ∠CDE (alternate interior, AB ∥ DC); △ABE ≅ △CDE (ASA); corresponding sides. S25-M-Q2.skill: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other

S25-M-Q3.skill: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other

S25-M-Q3.required_method: Show the two diagonals have the same midpoint.

S25-M-Q4.skill: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other

A proof that the diagonals of parallelogram ABCD bisect each other (they meet at E):
1. AB = CD  (?)
2. ∠BAE ≅ ∠DCE  (?)
3. ∠AEB ≅ ∠CED  (?)
4. △ABE ≅ △CDE  (?)
5. AE = CE, BE = DE  (?)
Give the five reasons.
S25-M-Q4.correct_answer: 1: opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent; 2: alternate interior angles (AB ∥ DC); 3: vertical angles; 4: AAS; 5: corresponding parts.

S26-M-Q1.skill: Prove the converses: conditions that make a quadrilateral a parallelogram

S26-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: SSS (AB = CD, BC = DA, AC shared); ∠BAC ≅ ∠DCA, so AB ∥ DC (converse); ∠BCA ≅ ∠DAC, so BC ∥ AD; definition. Invalid: using properties of parallelograms before proving it is one.
S26-M-Q1.required_method: Prove △ABC ≅ △CDA by SSS, then use the converse of the alternate interior angles theorem twice.

S26-M-Q2.skill: Prove the converses: conditions that make a quadrilateral a parallelogram
S26-M-Q2.prompt: In quadrilateral ABCD, diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at E. Prove that ABCD is a parallelogram.
S26-M-Q2.correct_answer: AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC, so ABCD is a parallelogram.
S26-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: AE = CE, BE = DE (bisect); vertical angles; SAS twice; ∠EAB ≅ ∠ECD gives AB ∥ DC; ∠EAD ≅ ∠ECB gives AD ∥ BC.

S26-M-Q2.required_method: Prove △AEB ≅ △CED and △AED ≅ △CEB by SAS (vertical angles), then use congruent alternate interior angles.

S26-M-Q3.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: ∠BAC ≅ ∠DCA (alternate interior, AB ∥ DC); AB = CD; AC shared; SAS; ∠BCA ≅ ∠DAC; AD ∥ BC (converse).
S26-M-Q3.required_method: Draw diagonal AC; prove △ABC ≅ △CDA by SAS, then show AD ∥ BC.

S26-M-Q4.skill: Prove the converses: conditions that make a quadrilateral a parallelogram

S26-M-Q4.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: 2m∠A + 2m∠B = 360°, so m∠A + m∠B = 180°; same-side interior angles supplementary gives AD ∥ BC; similarly m∠A + m∠D = 180° gives AB ∥ DC.
S26-M-Q4.required_method: Use the quadrilateral angle sum to show consecutive angles are supplementary, then the converse of the same-side interior angles theorem.

S53-M-Q1.skill: Prove that all circles are similar
S53-M-Q1.prompt: Circle C has center A and radius r, and circle D has center B and radius s. Prove that the two circles are similar.
S53-M-Q1.correct_answer: A translation followed by a dilation maps C onto D, so they are similar.
S53-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: (1) the translation maps C onto the circle with center B and radius r (distances kept); (2) the dilation about B with factor s/r maps each point at distance r from B to a point at distance s on the same ray, so onto D; (3) every point of D is reached (the inverse dilation); a similarity transformation exists. Invalid: "circles all look alike"; only checking two specific circles.
S53-M-Q1.required_method: Translate A to B, then dilate about B with scale factor s/r. Show the image of C is exactly D.

S53-M-Q2.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: the translation (x, y) → (x - 5, y - 2) moves the center to (-4, 0) keeping the radius 3; the dilation about (-4, 0) by 2 doubles every distance from the center, so radius 6.

S95-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: |√((x + 5)² + y²) - √((x - 5)² + y²)| = 6; isolate and square; simplify to 5x - 9 = ±3√((x - 5)² + y²) (or equivalent); square again; 16x² - 9y² = 144.
S95-M-Q1.required_method: Write the distance difference, isolate one radical, square twice, and simplify.

S96-M-Q1.skill: Use Cavalieri's principle to justify the volume of a sphere
S96-M-Q1.prompt: A hemisphere of radius r and a cylinder of radius r and height r with a cone removed (as shown) sit on the same plane. Use Cavalieri's principle to show that the hemisphere's volume is ⅔πr³, and conclude that a sphere has volume 4/3 πr³.
S96-M-Q1.correct_answer: Both cross-sections have area π(r² - y²), so the volumes are equal: πr³ - ⅓πr³ = ⅔πr³; the sphere is two hemispheres: 4/3 πr³.
S96-M-Q1.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: hemisphere slice radius √(r² - y²) (Pythagorean), area π(r² - y²); the other slice is a ring with outer radius r and inner radius y (the cone radius at height y), area πr² - πy²; equal areas at every height and equal heights; Cavalieri; volume cylinder minus cone = ⅔πr³; double.

Right: a cylinder of radius r and height r with an upside-down cone (vertex at the center of the bottom, base at the top) removed, shown in side view, with a dashed slice at the same height y.

S96-M-Q1.required_method: Compare the cross-section areas at height y.
